Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $T$ be the event that a customer is a teenager, $S$ be the event that a customer is satisfied, and ${P}_{1},{P}_{2},{P}_{3}$ be the event that a customer bought the product on platform $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({P}_{1})=0.56 &  & P(S|{P}_{1})=0.96 \\  & P({P}_{2})=0.14 &  & P(S|{P}_{2})=0.8 \\  & P({P}_{3})=0.3 &  & P(S|{P}_{3})=0.9\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${P}_{1}⊔{P}_{2}⊔{P}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({P}_{1})+P({P}_{2})+P({P}_{3})=0.56+0.14+0.3=1.
$$

- Since $45%$ of all customers are teenagers, we have

$$
P(T)=0.45.
$$

- Since $92%$ of teenage customers are satisfied, we have

$$
P(S|T)=0.92.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen satisfied customer is a teenager, which is represented as $P(T|S).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(T|S) & =\frac{P(S|T)P(T)}{P(S)} \\  & =\frac{P(S|T)P(T)}{P(S|{P}_{1})P({P}_{1})+P(S|{P}_{2})P({P}_{2})+P(S|{P}_{3})P({P}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.92)(0.45)}{(0.96)(0.56)+(0.8)(0.14)+(0.9)(0.3)} \\  & =\frac{0.414}{0.9196} \\  & ≈0.450,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c73be3d6-f9cd-557f-808f-32f2584f9bbf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c73be3d6-f9cd-557f-808f-32f2584f9bbf" :answer-field/id #uuid "c73be3d6-f9cd-557f-808f-32f2584f9bbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c14f8a89-fea0-54b9-b1c5-9f5e4448898b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3c8f2023-1fee-54ee-b839-16e84ad33b05" "answer-8e350e9f-716f-532f-bd7a-2341e751c264" "answer-1ec3078b-e60d-54c6-b2c0-e39ab1d2818a" "answer-c14f8a89-fea0-54b9-b1c5-9f5e4448898b" "answer-7ba26f79-d043-5412-9c51-78634aa91c09"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c8f2023-1fee-54ee-b839-16e84ad33b05" :answer/id #uuid "3c8f2023-1fee-54ee-b839-16e84ad33b05" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.124" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e350e9f-716f-532f-bd7a-2341e751c264" :answer/id #uuid "8e350e9f-716f-532f-bd7a-2341e751c264" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.355" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ec3078b-e60d-54c6-b2c0-e39ab1d2818a" :answer/id #uuid "1ec3078b-e60d-54c6-b2c0-e39ab1d2818a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.372" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c14f8a89-fea0-54b9-b1c5-9f5e4448898b" :answer/id #uuid "c14f8a89-fea0-54b9-b1c5-9f5e4448898b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.450" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ba26f79-d043-5412-9c51-78634aa91c09" :answer/id #uuid "7ba26f79-d043-5412-9c51-78634aa91c09" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.485" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f7a1a1db-a551-5627-b716-a412f2910020" :question/id #uuid "f7a1a1db-a551-5627-b716-a412f2910020" :question/math-academy-id "q-149492" :question/problem "A volleyball school for children splits the players into three teams, team $1,$ team $2,$ and team $3.$

- $54%$ of the children are in team $1,$ and $20%$ of players in this team have been playing volleyball for over a year.

- $32%$ of the children are in team $2,$ and $30%$ of players in this team have been playing volleyball for over a year.

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $B$ be the event that a child can play in all positions, $I$ be the event that a child has been playing for over a year, and ${T}_{1},{T}_{2},{T}_{3}$ be the events that a child is in team $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({T}_{1})=0.54 &  & P(I|{T}_{1})=0.2 \\  & P({T}_{2})=0.32 &  & P(I|{T}_{2})=0.3 \\  & P({T}_{3})=0.14 &  & P(I|{T}_{3})=0.15\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${T}_{1}⊔{T}_{2}⊔{T}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.54+0.32+0.15=1.
$$

- Since $10%$ of children can play in all positions, we have

$$
P(B)=0.1.
$$

- Since $94%$ of children who play in all positions have been playing for over a year, we have

$$
P(I|B)=0.94.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child who has been playing for over a year can play in all positions, which is represented as $P(B|I).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I)} \\  & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I|{T}_{1})P({T}_{1})+P(I|{T}_{2})P({T}_{2})+P(I|{T}_{3})P({T}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.94)(0.1)}{(0.2)(0.54)+(0.3)(0.32)+(0.15)(0.14)} \\  & =\frac{0.094}{0.225} \\  & ≈0.418,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-da0d6d19-9eb1-5179-970a-8af07c710dc1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-da0d6d19-9eb1-5179-970a-8af07c710dc1" :answer-field/id #uuid "da0d6d19-9eb1-5179-970a-8af07c710dc1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d344ed22-0120-51f9-b42a-cedaf01ced46" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b41e43a3-a236-598c-b879-c1d73ef7060d" "answer-d344ed22-0120-51f9-b42a-cedaf01ced46" "answer-5891b082-1b99-5e53-b911-542f283ae193" "answer-1b8c05fe-cf34-5642-b9f4-e1a31950c02d" "answer-092fec60-965b-5d2f-b7c9-4af5092da86b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b41e43a3-a236-598c-b879-c1d73ef7060d" :answer/id #uuid "b41e43a3-a236-598c-b879-c1d73ef7060d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.323" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d344ed22-0120-51f9-b42a-cedaf01ced46" :answer/id #uuid "d344ed22-0120-51f9-b42a-cedaf01ced46" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.418" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5891b082-1b99-5e53-b911-542f283ae193" :answer/id #uuid "5891b082-1b99-5e53-b911-542f283ae193" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.482" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b8c05fe-cf34-5642-b9f4-e1a31950c02d" :answer/id #uuid "1b8c05fe-cf34-5642-b9f4-e1a31950c02d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.529" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-092fec60-965b-5d2f-b7c9-4af5092da86b" :answer/id #uuid "092fec60-965b-5d2f-b7c9-4af5092da86b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.582" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167119 :question/problem "Arthur and Sara are finding the best recipe for chocolate muffins, and they test three different oven cooking modes, mode $1,$ mode $2,$ and mode $3.$ They also try two types of yeast, A and B.

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a muffin is made with yeast A, $G$ be the event that a muffin turns out well, and ${M}_{1},{M}_{2},{M}_{3}$ be the event that a muffin is cooked with mode $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({M}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(G|{M}_{1})=0.8 \\  & P({M}_{2})=0.35 &  & P(G|{M}_{2}) \\  & P({M}_{3})=0.2 &  & P(G|{M}_{3})=0.9\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${M}_{1}⊔{M}_{2}⊔{M}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({M}_{1})+P({M}_{2})+P({M}_{3})=0.45+0.35+0.2=1.
$$

- Since $65%$ of muffins are made with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.65.
$$

- Since $82%$ of muffins made with yeast A turned out well, we have

$$
P(G|A)=0.82.
$$

- Since $68%$ of good muffins were prepared with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A|G)=0.68.

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen muffin cooked with mode $2$ turned well, which is represented as $P(G|{M}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G)} \\ P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G|{M}_{1})P({M}_{1})+P(G|{M}_{2})P({M}_{2})+P(G|{M}_{3})P({M}_{3})} \\ 0.68 & =\frac{(0.82)(0.65)}{(0.8)(0.45)+P(G|{M}_{2})(0.35)+(0.9)(0.2)} \\ 0.68 & =\frac{0.533}{0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(G|{M}_{2}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.68(0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54) & =0.533 \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54 & =\frac{0.533}{0.68} \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54 & =\frac{533}{680} \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2}) & =\frac{533}{680}-0.54 \\ P(G|{M}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.35}(\frac{533}{680}-0.54) \\ P(G|{M}_{2}) & ≈0.697\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $g(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[-4,-1]$ and differentiable on  $(-4,-1).$

Given that $g(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem states the following: 

> *There exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*

$$
{g}^{′}(c)=\frac{g(b)-g(a)}{b-a}.
$$

In our case, we have $a=-4$ and $b=-1.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(c) & =\frac{g(-1)-g(-4)}{-1-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{1-(-1)}{-1+4} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

>  *The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c\in (-4,-1)$ such that ${g}^{′}(c)=\frac{2}{3}.$*" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/id #uuid "af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer/id #uuid "61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092390 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/id #uuid "93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/math-academy-id "q-166148" :question/problem "Given that $f(2.1)=21,$ approximate ${f}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=2.1$ using a backward difference approximation.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we differentiate $x=\frac{3}{5y-2}$ with respect to $y:$

two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x, & \,0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}3y, & \,0\le y\le \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\le 0.5,Y\le \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}).$" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =2x\cdot 3y \\  & =6xy,\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,1]\times [1,\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}6xy, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 0.5,Y\le 1) & ={\int }_{0}^{0.5}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2/3}}6xy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0.5}6x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{2/3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0.5}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{0.5} \\  & =(0.5)^{2}-0 \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185490 :answer-field/correct 17592186185493 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188561 :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}y, & \,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(0\le X\le 0.4,Y\le 2).$ Round your answer to three decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}y \\  & =y\sqrt{x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,1]\times [1,2].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}y\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le X\le 0.4,Y\le 2) & ={\int }_{0}^{0.4}[{\int }_{1}^{2}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0.4}\sqrt{x}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0.4}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{0.4} \\  & =(0.4)^{3/2}-0 \\  & ≈0.253.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185646 :answer-field/correct 17592186185650 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-1706fef5-2c32-54fe-bdcf-eb9228266f86" :question/id #uuid "1706fef5-2c32-54fe-bdcf-eb9228266f86" :question/math-academy-id "q-143364" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}, & \,0\le x, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}y, & \,3\le y\le 5, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\ge 2,3\le Y\le 4).$" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={e}^{-x}\cdot \frac{1}{8}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}y{e}^{-x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,\infty )\times [3,5].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}y{e}^{-x}, & \,0\le x,\,3\le y\le 5 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2,3\le Y\le 4) & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }[{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{8}y{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{8}{e}^{-x}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{3}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{7}{16}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{b}\frac{7}{16}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{7{e}^{-x}}{16}]}_{2}^{b} \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }[-\frac{7{e}^{-b}}{16}+\frac{7{e}^{-2}}{16}] \\  & =\frac{7}{16{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1b00f6e3-8cc3-5080-b638-0c0a437c40d6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/problem "The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{Y}(y)=\frac{2}{3}y$ for $y\in [1,2]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{3}y{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}y,\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [1,2].$

- Statement II is true. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4{x}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,1].$ So, when $x\in [0,1]$ and $y\in [1,2],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}={{(4{x}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{(\frac{2}{3}y)}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-54963578-cc23-5bef-b243-20d224d918a2"] :db/ensure :question/problem "The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}(x+y),\, & 1\le x\le 2,\,2\le y\le 3, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{Y}(y)=\frac{1}{4}(y+\frac{3}{2})$ for $y\in [2,3]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{4}(x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+yx]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2+2y-\frac{1}{2}-y) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(y+\frac{3}{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [2,3].$

- Statement II is false. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{4}(x+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=2}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3x+\frac{9}{2}-2x-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(x+\frac{5}{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [1,2].$ So, when $x\in [1,2]$ and $y\in [2,3],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{\frac{1}{4}(x+y)}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}\ne {{\frac{1}{4}(x+\frac{5}{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{\frac{1}{4}(y+\frac{3}{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is *not* true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9e41b8cd-f547-56b5-b624-9d4998a39501"] :db/ensure - the graph of $y=f(x-k)$ is a horizontal translation of $y=f(x)$ by $k$ units to the *right*, while

- the graph of $y=f(x+k)$ is a horizontal translation of $y=f(x)$ by $k$ units to the *left*.

**Watch out!** It may seem counterintuitive that subtracting $k$ moves the graph to the right, while adding $k$ moves the graph to the left. However, this is in fact true.

To see why, let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below. Let's use this graph to plot the graph of $y=f(x-2).$

![](images/6c/6ca96bba855899f9b87ae06c166503c9af739fcd6bb2ec466a73b75cc70dde7f.png)

Let's take some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ and find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(x-2).$ 

For example, take the point $(3,-4).$ The fact that it's on the graph of $y=f(x)$ means that $f(3)=-4.$ Then if $x={\color{red}5},$ we have 

$$
f(x-2) = f({\color{red}5}-2) = f(3) = -4,
$$

 
which means that $({\color{red}5},-4)$ is on the graph of $y=f(x-2).$ 

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ with the same $y$-value and a $x$-value that is $2$ units *greater*! Several more examples of points are shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=f(x-2)[/math]} \\ (3,-4) & (5,-4) \\ (1,2) & (3,2) \\ (0,1.5) & (2,1.5) \\ (-2,0) & (0,0)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's plot both curves.

![](images/ed/edae088984432dc7d0fff816a9e016ad221a3c897a78cf79efe6c784fa9176fe.png)

We see that every point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ is shifted $2$ units *to the right* of the corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115418 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=2$ and $y=3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+7z & =-9 \\ 3(2)+2(3)+7z & =-9 \\ 7z & =-21 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,-3⟩-⟨5,9,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-6,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,2,7⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-3)\cdot 3+(-6)\cdot 2+3\cdot 7|}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{7}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-9-12+21|}{\sqrt{9+4+49}} \\  & =\frac{|\,0\,|}{\sqrt{62}} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $P$ lies on the plane." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186117659 :answer-field/correct 17592186117662 :db/ensure ["question-a24feddb-3c6c-5b5d-be09-ecb6ef41d845"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096400 :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f = g^5, \qquad g = 3x^4+x^3
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g}  = 5g^4,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x} = 12x^3 + 3x^2.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =5{g}^{4}\cdot (12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =5(3{x}^{4}+{x}^{3})^{4}(12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096842 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-45936e93-e188-5489-9cc9-795dad15e0d6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096402 :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)=1-3x$ and $f(g(x)) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}} = g^{-1/2}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{-1/2})^{′}=-\frac{1}{2}{g}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2{g}^{3/2}}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(1-3x)^{′}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{g}^{3/2}}\cdot (-3) \\  & =\frac{3}{2{g}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{2(1-3x)^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a24feddb-3c6c-5b5d-be09-ecb6ef41d845" :question/id #uuid "a24feddb-3c6c-5b5d-be09-ecb6ef41d845" :question/math-academy-id "q-48622" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=(3{x}^{2}-10)^{4},$ find the slope at the point $(2,16).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f={g}^{4},\,g=3{x}^{2}-10
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4{g}^{3},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=6x.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (6x) \\  & =24x(3{x}^{2}-10)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at the point where $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={24x{(3{x}^{2}-10)}^{3}|}_{x=2} \\  & =24(2){(3(2)^{2}-10)}^{3} \\  & =384.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a15449d-4ef5-5450-8663-fb7daf5af1c5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}$ at the point where $x=-1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (6x+2) \\  & =\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=-1} \\  & =\frac{6(-1)+2}{2\sqrt{3(-1)^{2}+2(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f05471f2-c115-5266-86b4-2c4bebd70c45"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f05471f2-c115-5266-86b4-2c4bebd70c45" :answer-field/id #uuid "f05471f2-c115-5266-86b4-2c4bebd70c45" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-bc8d190d-9c67-5acd-8583-f14a36220ea6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc8d190d-9c67-5acd-8583-f14a36220ea6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc8d190d-9c67-5acd-8583-f14a36220ea6" :answer/id #uuid "bc8d190d-9c67-5acd-8583-f14a36220ea6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186339021 :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)=8x-7$ and $f(g(x))=g(x)^{4}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{4})^{′}=4{g}^{3}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(8x-7)^{′}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (8) \\  & =32(8x-7)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186338377 :answer-field/correct "answer-25c6804e-8060-5dff-bba1-acaf4df961ab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d56bf506-fd8c-5071-aec9-cd4f69c5a6e1" "answer-a07a2ebe-3a0b-54c5-a1a1-e83b39b74dac" "answer-a9e6700f-f254-59c8-947f-7f6a658e28f1" "answer-25c6804e-8060-5dff-bba1-acaf4df961ab" "answer-ee2fea0e-928b-58ba-8851-272406927771"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d56bf506-fd8c-5071-aec9-cd4f69c5a6e1" :answer/id #uuid "d56bf506-fd8c-5071-aec9-cd4f69c5a6e1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16(16x-7)^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a07a2ebe-3a0b-54c5-a1a1-e83b39b74dac" :answer/id #uuid "a07a2ebe-3a0b-54c5-a1a1-e83b39b74dac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16(8x-7)^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a9e6700f-f254-59c8-947f-7f6a658e28f1" :answer/id #uuid "a9e6700f-f254-59c8-947f-7f6a658e28f1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32(16x-7)^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25c6804e-8060-5dff-bba1-acaf4df961ab" :answer/id #uuid "25c6804e-8060-5dff-bba1-acaf4df961ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32(8x-7)^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee2fea0e-928b-58ba-8851-272406927771" :answer/id #uuid "ee2fea0e-928b-58ba-8851-272406927771" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8(8x-7)^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097259 :question/problem "Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for $f(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+3x}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)=2{x}^{2}+3x$ and $f(g(x))=\frac{2}{\sqrt{g}}=2{g}^{-1/2}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =2({g}^{-1/2})^{′}=-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{g}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{{g}^{3/2}}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(2{x}^{2}+3x)^{′}=4x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{g}^{3/2}}\cdot (4x+3) \\  & =-\frac{4x+3}{{g}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{4x+3}{\sqrt{(2{x}^{2}+3x)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = f'(g(a)) \cdot g'(a)
$$

Let $f$ and $g$ be functions such that

- $g$ is differentiable at $a$,

- $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$.

Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $a$, and we compute its derivative as follows.

We start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a}
$$

Since $g$ is differentiable at $a$, it is also continuous there. Hence $g(x) \to g(a)$ as $x \to a$. For $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, we have $g(x) \ne g(a)$, so we may write

$$
\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a} 
= \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{g(x) - g(a)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}.
$$

Taking the limit as $x \to a$, and using the product rule for limits (which applies since both limits exist), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘g)^{′}(a) & ={lim}_{x\to a}(\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot \frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot {lim}_{x\to a}\frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a} \\  & ={f}^{′}(g(a))\cdot {g}^{′}(a)\end{aligned}
$$

as required." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096888 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176417 :question/problem "What is the equation of the line that passes through the point $(1,-5)$ and is perpendicular to $x+3y=12?$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation $x+3y=12$ in its slope-intercept form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+3y & =12 \\ 3y & =-x+12 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of the new line should be the negative reciprocal of the slope of the given line $y=-\frac{1}{3}x+4.$ The given line has a slope of $-\frac{1}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $3.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=3$ and pass through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(1,-5).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-5) & =3(x-1) \\ y+5 & =3x-3 \\ y & =3x-8\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186174740 :answer-field/correct "answer-ccac27b1-4d1c-5479-8665-d033a45d1913" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ccac27b1-4d1c-5479-8665-d033a45d1913"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ccac27b1-4d1c-5479-8665-d033a45d1913" :answer/id #uuid "ccac27b1-4d1c-5479-8665-d033a45d1913" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3x-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175923 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d79473d6-bc2e-50df-aa4f-f2c7866c75c4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d79473d6-bc2e-50df-aa4f-f2c7866c75c4" :question/id #uuid "d79473d6-bc2e-50df-aa4f-f2c7866c75c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-237034" :question/problem "Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(4,-1)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(2,3)$ and $(-4,2).$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(2,3)$ and $(-4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{2-3}{-4-2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)}{(-6)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{1}{6})=-1\,⇒\,m=-6.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(4,-1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-1) & =-6(x-4) \\ y+1 & =-6x+24 \\ y & =-6x+23\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-618796c9-d723-5e11-9f71-2d4878c12e36"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-618796c9-d723-5e11-9f71-2d4878c12e36" :answer-field/id #uuid "618796c9-d723-5e11-9f71-2d4878c12e36" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-cba90753-0239-53f3-8288-4708dc4bd2d7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cba90753-0239-53f3-8288-4708dc4bd2d7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cba90753-0239-53f3-8288-4708dc4bd2d7" :answer/id #uuid "cba90753-0239-53f3-8288-4708dc4bd2d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6x+23" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "activity-dce5a6b1-8e80-58c8-af08-9ef023487bbb" :activity/id #uuid "dce5a6b1-8e80-58c8-af08-9ef023487bbb" :activity/title "Finding Equations of Perpendicular Lines" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186050473 :activity/course 17592186046647 :activity/steps ["step-1eab4d5a-96a8-544b-91f1-6e63e881567a" "step-91ab80b6-9654-58b5-aeba-94ac364e8346" "step-f8031d83-20ce-5562-9e78-310af75e7f3b"] :activity/first-step "step-1eab4d5a-96a8-544b-91f1-6e63e881567a" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-1eab4d5a-96a8-544b-91f1-6e63e881567a" :step/id #uuid "1eab4d5a-96a8-544b-91f1-6e63e881567a" :step/content 17592186238009 :step/next "step-91ab80b6-9654-58b5-aeba-94ac364e8346" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-91ab80b6-9654-58b5-aeba-94ac364e8346" :step/id #uuid "91ab80b6-9654-58b5-aeba-94ac364e8346" :step/content 17592186176417 :step/next "step-f8031d83-20ce-5562-9e78-310af75e7f3b" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-f8031d83-20ce-5562-9e78-310af75e7f3b" :step/id #uuid "f8031d83-20ce-5562-9e78-310af75e7f3b" :step/content "question-d79473d6-bc2e-50df-aa4f-f2c7866c75c4" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176287 :question/problem "Given that the random variables

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(2,{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(20,{5}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(6,5),
$$

and

$$
Y=10{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2}+5{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =10\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot 20+5\cdot 6 \\  & =-30, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={10}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}+{5}^{2}\cdot 5 \\  & =100\cdot 1+16\cdot 25+25\cdot 5 \\  & =625.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(-30,625).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3<Y<40).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =P(\frac{3-(-30)}{\sqrt{625}}<Z<\frac{40-(-30)}{\sqrt{625}}) \\  & =P(1.32<Z<2.8) \\  & =P(Z<2.8)-P(Z<1.32) \\  & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.32)≈0.9066,\,Φ(2.8)≈0.9974.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32) \\  & ≈0.9974-0.9066 \\  & ≈0.0908.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173980 :answer-field/correct 17592186173981 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176038 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aeaa1356-185b-56a9-b08f-e66f177f60f6" "question-bb2b4349-d915-5c8e-b7b7-7b70ca85595f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-aeaa1356-185b-56a9-b08f-e66f177f60f6" :question/id #uuid "aeaa1356-185b-56a9-b08f-e66f177f60f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-142953" :question/problem "Given that the random variables

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then

$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3+1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =-3-2-3 \\  & =-8, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & =(-1)^{2}\cdot 1+{1}^{2}\cdot 7+(-1)^{2}\cdot 4 \\  & =1\cdot 1+1\cdot 7+1\cdot 4 \\  & =1+7+4 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-67ddbf3e-4217-58b2-b747-80503cb6e6d9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-67ddbf3e-4217-58b2-b747-80503cb6e6d9" :answer-field/id #uuid "67ddbf3e-4217-58b2-b747-80503cb6e6d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7a5ba93e-4108-5fae-9897-dfdc52f0d17b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7a5ba93e-4108-5fae-9897-dfdc52f0d17b" "answer-7c930188-07ec-5cf7-8f0c-30a82ea69ebc" "answer-3cd5666e-b1a6-5c93-80fa-6b640a8a153c" "answer-32947573-91b6-5876-8f57-de94fd70326c" "answer-17a06aae-ac2c-529c-a4a8-54293cbc5294"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7a5ba93e-4108-5fae-9897-dfdc52f0d17b" :answer/id #uuid "7a5ba93e-4108-5fae-9897-dfdc52f0d17b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Y∼N(-8,12)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c930188-07ec-5cf7-8f0c-30a82ea69ebc" :answer/id #uuid "7c930188-07ec-5cf7-8f0c-30a82ea69ebc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Y∼N(-8,28)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3cd5666e-b1a6-5c93-80fa-6b640a8a153c" :answer/id #uuid "3cd5666e-b1a6-5c93-80fa-6b640a8a153c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Y∼N(4,6)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32947573-91b6-5876-8f57-de94fd70326c" :answer/id #uuid "32947573-91b6-5876-8f57-de94fd70326c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Y∼N(8,12)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-17a06aae-ac2c-529c-a4a8-54293cbc5294" :answer/id #uuid "17a06aae-ac2c-529c-a4a8-54293cbc5294" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Y∼N(8,28)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-bb2b4349-d915-5c8e-b7b7-7b70ca85595f" :question/id #uuid "bb2b4349-d915-5c8e-b7b7-7b70ca85595f" :question/math-academy-id "q-142954" :question/problem "Given that the random variables

a box.  The weight of a single muffin is normally distributed with a mean of $33\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $10\,{\text{g}}^{2},$ while the weight of a box is normally distributed with a mean of $20\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $5\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$  

If a box with two muffins is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $90\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ | $\,0.8264\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the weight of the two muffins, and the box, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(33,10),\,{X}_{2}∼N(33,10),\,{X}_{3}∼N(20,5).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the weight of the box with muffins. Then, we have

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =2\cdot 33+20 \\  & =86, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =2\cdot 10+5 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ∼N(86,25).\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $P(Y>90),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>90) & =P(Z>\frac{90-86}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z>0.8) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.8) \\  & =1-Φ(0.80)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.80)≈0.7881.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>90) & =1-Φ(0.8) \\  & ≈1-0.7881 \\  & =0.2119.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2735551e-9e10-5c27-940a-16893a72cfc7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2735551e-9e10-5c27-940a-16893a72cfc7" :answer-field/id #uuid "2735551e-9e10-5c27-940a-16893a72cfc7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d7661f2b-95e9-5000-bfe5-76a1ad216e55" :answer-field/choices ["answer-affae556-27d5-59ef-ac47-5a6ae5fa86f4" "answer-d7661f2b-95e9-5000-bfe5-76a1ad216e55" "answer-0a064c83-9501-54cc-854f-6385f084792d" "answer-dc21b836-4901-5804-9c1f-adc4b7b07bde" "answer-f9506774-0343-5070-8358-9d5f49af130e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-affae556-27d5-59ef-ac47-5a6ae5fa86f4" :answer/id #uuid "affae556-27d5-59ef-ac47-5a6ae5fa86f4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2033" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7661f2b-95e9-5000-bfe5-76a1ad216e55" :answer/id #uuid "d7661f2b-95e9-5000-bfe5-76a1ad216e55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2119" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a064c83-9501-54cc-854f-6385f084792d" :answer/id #uuid "0a064c83-9501-54cc-854f-6385f084792d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2296" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dc21b836-4901-5804-9c1f-adc4b7b07bde" :answer/id #uuid "dc21b836-4901-5804-9c1f-adc4b7b07bde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2389" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f9506774-0343-5070-8358-9d5f49af130e" :answer/id #uuid "f9506774-0343-5070-8358-9d5f49af130e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2743" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f066bbcb-f1c2-5b35-9178-0754e305b471" :question/id #uuid "f066bbcb-f1c2-5b35-9178-0754e305b471" :question/math-academy-id "q-143103" :question/problem "A wireless headphone set includes $2$ earbuds (left and right) and a charging case.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,[-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\sqrt[4]{x})] \\  & =-2\cdot [-\frac{1}{|\sqrt[4]{x}|\sqrt{1+{(\sqrt[4]{x})}^{2}}}]\cdot {(\sqrt[4]{x})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[4]{x}\sqrt{1+\sqrt{x}}}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt[4]{{x}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{1+\sqrt{x}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f068fa89-ce05-5148-b62a-30202a76bdb3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f068fa89-ce05-5148-b62a-30202a76bdb3" :answer-field/id #uuid "f068fa89-ce05-5148-b62a-30202a76bdb3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-93683338-b97b-5b47-8572-b2056cda9e98" :answer-field/choices ["answer-93683338-b97b-5b47-8572-b2056cda9e98"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93683338-b97b-5b47-8572-b2056cda9e98" :answer/id #uuid "93683338-b97b-5b47-8572-b2056cda9e98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{1+\sqrt{x}}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167378 :question/problem "$$

$\frac{1}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡(2x-1)}$" :question/worked-solution "In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1).$

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1))^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡(2x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1)}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡(2x-1)}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1))^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡(2x-1)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1)}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1))^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡(2x-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)=\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},

$$
(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2x-1))^{′}=\frac{1}{1-(2x-1)^{2}}\cdot (2x-1)^{′}=\frac{2}{4x-4{x}^{2}}.

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186296661 :answer-field/correct "answer-f54d10f9-87ce-520f-be5c-16afa4e5c6a2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f54d10f9-87ce-520f-be5c-16afa4e5c6a2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f54d10f9-87ce-520f-be5c-16afa4e5c6a2" :answer/id #uuid "f54d10f9-87ce-520f-be5c-16afa4e5c6a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\cdot8^{x}\ln(8)+12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097815 :tutorial/content "To derive the identity

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x,
$$

we begin with the definition of the derivative:

where $f(x) = e^x$.

Substituting the function $f(x)$ into the definition of $f'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x+h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot ({e}^{h}-1)}{h} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{h}-1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$
f'(x) = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096892 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221456 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9b306e59-ac03-5a23-8563-3ae450882f03" "question-234b7e73-d01a-5fb8-b7f2-7b7733987672"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-9b306e59-ac03-5a23-8563-3ae450882f03" :question/id #uuid "9b306e59-ac03-5a23-8563-3ae450882f03" :question/math-academy-id "q-343882" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-5\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-5)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=5 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-5)=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=-\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+20)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+20)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e37207bf-0563-5832-ad30-c6a23c3c930c" "answer-field-8f9455a9-07ca-5997-b4ca-16fa2b6ab07c"] :db/ensure #uuid "234b7e73-d01a-5fb8-b7f2-7b7733987672" :question/math-academy-id "q-343886" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-10y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-10(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=10 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)=\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-04a2bae6-aeac-5a01-8bbe-2da7affb6702" "answer-field-3b8556e9-1a54-5d0b-a5a5-5efa77eeb553"] :db/ensure "1741c2e1-8000-5ded-a8b9-94a357d2c64a" :question/math-academy-id "q-343887" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=0 \\ 3\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{27\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{27\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-65f9587c-2102-51c3-9018-cf73e669ee77" "answer-field-b41532f6-c5f8-55db-9dde-0e3b62dd91b0"] :db/ensure $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[0,10],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}, & 0\le x\le 10 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<X<7) & ={\int }_{3}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{7}\frac{1}{10}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{10}|}_{3}^{7} \\  & =\frac{7}{10}-\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}

$$

From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U[52,66],$ and we wish to compute $P(X\le 60).$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[52,66],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{14}, & 52\le x\le 66 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 60) & ={\int }_{52}^{60}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{52}^{60}\frac{1}{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{14}|}_{52}^{60} \\  & =\frac{60}{14}-\frac{52}{14} \\  & =\frac{4}{7}.\end{aligned}

![](images/93/93894f939fa0ef715ee6ab6c225f456972b746184673df0b8d8312656727d793.svg)

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution: 

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/fd/fd37b3e19aad197ebb7eeabad00fca068455eed8da462a12630134cd7980941e.svg)

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean waiting time is $10$ minutes." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157536 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221445 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6138bd37-a9a0-5af4-80eb-ad7aa981c99c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222023 :question/problem "$$

$$

Let $F(x)=6x+1$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{5}.$

${b}_{5}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=6x+1$ for $x\in (-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{5}=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(6x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{3}{5\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{5} & =\frac{1}{3}(uv\,{|}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{3}{5\pi }{[(6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}+\frac{18}{5\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(-{[(6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}+6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(-((6(3)+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi )-(6(-3)+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-5\pi ))+\frac{18}{5\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(36+\frac{18}{5\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-5\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }\cdot 36 \\  & =\frac{36}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186220816 :answer-field/correct "answer-b9caddf0-8911-56aa-9169-d2dd07b18d7d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b9caddf0-8911-56aa-9169-d2dd07b18d7d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9caddf0-8911-56aa-9169-d2dd07b18d7d" :answer/id #uuid "b9caddf0-8911-56aa-9169-d2dd07b18d7d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{36}{5\pi}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221444 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-53537d13-56ed-578b-89f6-12be53184c9c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186372798 :answer-field/correct "answer-e65592e2-0cd5-534f-88d7-0eb0fc781f52" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e65592e2-0cd5-534f-88d7-0eb0fc781f52"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e65592e2-0cd5-534f-88d7-0eb0fc781f52" :answer/id #uuid "e65592e2-0cd5-534f-88d7-0eb0fc781f52" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi^2}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-53537d13-56ed-578b-89f6-12be53184c9c" :question/id #uuid "53537d13-56ed-578b-89f6-12be53184c9c" :question/math-academy-id "q-341808" :question/problem "$$

II. $(1-2x)-(2-{x}^{2})$

III. $(x+1)\cdot (4-{x}^{2})$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression I is a polynomial. It's a sum of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under addition.

- Expression II is a polynomial. It's a difference between two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under subtraction.

- Expression III gives a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8f34e0d0-1b01-548e-8ace-ce5ffc57a3fe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8f34e0d0-1b01-548e-8ace-ce5ffc57a3fe" :answer-field/id #uuid "8f34e0d0-1b01-548e-8ace-ce5ffc57a3fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-73340f47-6707-588d-91fe-a6db909018b2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-62b3d276-65bb-589c-bef8-28434c7b3a4e" "answer-a3288bcb-72e7-5d83-920c-df3c72f026c6" "answer-73340f47-6707-588d-91fe-a6db909018b2" "answer-731874e9-843e-5b25-9236-a231f2d5a98f" "answer-3bd31b5f-4edb-5614-90b1-3db842e42842"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-62b3d276-65bb-589c-bef8-28434c7b3a4e" :answer/id #uuid "62b3d276-65bb-589c-bef8-28434c7b3a4e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a3288bcb-72e7-5d83-920c-df3c72f026c6" :answer/id #uuid "a3288bcb-72e7-5d83-920c-df3c72f026c6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-73340f47-6707-588d-91fe-a6db909018b2" :answer/id #uuid "73340f47-6707-588d-91fe-a6db909018b2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-731874e9-843e-5b25-9236-a231f2d5a98f" :answer/id #uuid "731874e9-843e-5b25-9236-a231f2d5a98f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3bd31b5f-4edb-5614-90b1-3db842e42842" :answer/id #uuid "3bd31b5f-4edb-5614-90b1-3db842e42842" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-83c42558-b7ba-54b4-8258-155dbb7534d4" :question/id #uuid "83c42558-b7ba-54b4-8258-155dbb7534d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-141239" :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

$$

$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

17592186162636 :question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are negative semi-definite?

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is *not* negative semi-definite since some of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ is positive).

- Quadratic form II is negative semi-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are non-positive.

- Quadratic form III is negative semi-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $S$ are non-positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161108 :answer-field/correct 17592186161113 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-aa5d7a51-2b25-530e-bc34-f2b29d7db7d9" :question/id #uuid "aa5d7a51-2b25-530e-bc34-f2b29d7db7d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-94788" :question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{3}$ are negative-definite?

"Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is positive-definite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-6,\,-4.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fc3a16ca-ab9d-5910-8403-1994cf7ec17a"] :db/ensure "question-7aa930b4-3c77-5008-aaf5-9bbf298703c7" :question/id #uuid "7aa930b4-3c77-5008-aaf5-9bbf298703c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94800" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${a}_{11}=-7$ and $det(A)=-3$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is positive-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-7$ and 

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-7 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=3.
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-7<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-7 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=3>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-079db36a-f121-5453-be8e-d40d62051237"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092118 :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 3\cdot 2^u, \qquad u=1-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 3\cdot 2^u\ln(2),\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092513 :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={e}^{2x+5},$ find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =2{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{2x+5}.\end{aligned}

$m=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=-2{x}^{7}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-14{x}^{6}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-14{x}^{6}) \\  & =-14{x}^{6}{e}^{u} \\  & =-14{x}^{6}{e}^{-2{x}^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(-14{x}^{6}{e}^{-2{x}^{7}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =-14(1)^{6}{e}^{-2(1)^{7}} \\  & =-14{e}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-11e1ae92-136f-5d68-8353-b8a4c9e485ce"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-11e1ae92-136f-5d68-8353-b8a4c9e485ce" :answer-field/id #uuid "11e1ae92-136f-5d68-8353-b8a4c9e485ce" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ca0e728f-63f5-5bf9-9222-2a283f84a906" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ca0e728f-63f5-5bf9-9222-2a283f84a906"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ca0e728f-63f5-5bf9-9222-2a283f84a906" :answer/id #uuid "ca0e728f-63f5-5bf9-9222-2a283f84a906" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{14}{e^2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-70b1c8a4-0636-5508-ab80-4e4e15ec81e5" :question/id #uuid "70b1c8a4-0636-5508-ab80-4e4e15ec81e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-340970" :question/problem "Find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve $y=2\cdot {5}^{1-3x}$ at the point where $x=0.$

$m=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=2\cdot {5}^{u},\,u=1-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=2\cdot {5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2\cdot {5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\cdot (-3) \\  & =-6\cdot {5}^{1-3x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(-6\cdot {5}^{1-3x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5)|}_{x=0} \\  & =-6\cdot {5}^{1-3(0)}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\  & =-6\cdot 5\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\  & =-30\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d83b75c0-fe56-5390-8126-bd377ed6af9e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d83b75c0-fe56-5390-8126-bd377ed6af9e" :answer-field/id #uuid "d83b75c0-fe56-5390-8126-bd377ed6af9e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ff3851f0-019b-54f0-9d24-526c6e29abe2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff3851f0-019b-54f0-9d24-526c6e29abe2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff3851f0-019b-54f0-9d24-526c6e29abe2" :answer/id #uuid "ff3851f0-019b-54f0-9d24-526c6e29abe2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-30\ln(5)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-77c551c0-c155-56eb-9f11-d8d660941796" :question/id #uuid "77c551c0-c155-56eb-9f11-d8d660941796" :question/math-academy-id "q-107463" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=-1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\cdot 2 \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point. 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡4)|}_{x=-1} \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((4)^{1/2}) \\  & =ln\,(\,\sqrt{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={({4}^{2x+1})|}_{x=-1} \\  & ={4}^{2(-1)+1} \\  & ={4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\cdot (x+1) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-717c0cdc-ae39-5590-87a2-a75a93baebfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id **Step 1**: Find the critical points:

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-3,3),$ and ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $x=0.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=-3,0,3.$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

The function is made up of $2$ rectangles and $2$ triangles. Let's add the areas bounded by these shapes to our diagram:

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(x-1)^{2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\ge 0 \\ (x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\le 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

which gives the interior of the ellipse $(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}=1$ and its boundary.

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\le 1\}.

Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8d768191-43c2-52ef-8bd4-abb5c4c7e134"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
