- They use mode $1$ to cook the $45%$ of their muffins, and $80%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $2$ to cook the $35%$ of their muffins.

- They use mode $3$ to cook the $20%$ of their muffins, and $90%$ of those muffins turn out well.

If $65%$ of all muffins were prepared with yeast A, $82%$ of yeast A muffins turn out well, and $68%$ of good muffins were prepared with yeast A, what is the probability that a randomly chosen muffin cooked with mode $2$ turned out well? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places."] [17592186167119 :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a muffin is made with yeast A, $G$ be the event that a muffin turns out well, and ${M}_{1},{M}_{2},{M}_{3}$ be the event that a muffin is cooked with mode $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({M}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(G|{M}_{1})=0.8 \\  & P({M}_{2})=0.35 &  & P(G|{M}_{2}) \\  & P({M}_{3})=0.2 &  & P(G|{M}_{3})=0.9\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${M}_{1}⊔{M}_{2}⊔{M}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({M}_{1})+P({M}_{2})+P({M}_{3})=0.45+0.35+0.2=1.
$$

- Since $65%$ of muffins are made with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.65.
$$

- Since $82%$ of muffins made with yeast A turned out well, we have

$$
P(G|A)=0.82.
$$

- Since $68%$ of good muffins were prepared with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A|G)=0.68.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen muffin cooked with mode $2$ turned well, which is represented as $P(G|{M}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G)} \\ P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G|{M}_{1})P({M}_{1})+P(G|{M}_{2})P({M}_{2})+P(G|{M}_{3})P({M}_{3})} \\ 0.68 & =\frac{(0.82)(0.65)}{(0.8)(0.45)+P(G|{M}_{2})(0.35)+(0.9)(0.2)} \\ 0.68 & =\frac{0.533}{0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(G|{M}_{2}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.68(0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54) & =0.533 \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54 & =\frac{0.533}{0.68} \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2})+0.54 & =\frac{533}{680} \\ 0.35P(G|{M}_{2}) & =\frac{533}{680}-0.54 \\ P(G|{M}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.35}(\frac{533}{680}-0.54) \\ P(G|{M}_{2}) & ≈0.697\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."] [17592186167119 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186163792 :answer-field/correct 17592186163797] ["question-08f35ffe-3316-51be-b28c-866b8f0d5426" :question/id #uuid "08f35ffe-3316-51be-b28c-866b8f0d5426"] ["question-08f35ffe-3316-51be-b28c-866b8f0d5426" :question/math-academy-id "q-166144"] ["question-08f35ffe-3316-51be-b28c-866b8f0d5426" :question/problem "Compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))$ at $x=2.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-2ad31a73-80bb-53e8-b8d5-84512ffb448a" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=-2$ directly into the limit, we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$

$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3f(x)-g(x)}{x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{{(3f(x)-g(x))}^{′}}{{(x+2)}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $x=-2$ again, and this time, we are able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-2}[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)] & ={[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)]|}_{x=-2} \\  & =3{f}^{′}(-2)-{g}^{′}(-2) \\  & =3\cdot 12-(-4) \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-caea6f22-353c-51f3-b53e-c4874e2c30a8" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $g(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[-4,-1]$ and differentiable on  $(-4,-1).$

Given that $g(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem states the following: 

> *There exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*

$$
{g}^{′}(c)=\frac{g(b)-g(a)}{b-a}.
$$

In our case, we have $a=-4$ and $b=-1.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(c) & =\frac{g(-1)-g(-4)}{-1-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{1-(-1)}{-1+4} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

>  *The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c\in (-4,-1)$ such that ${g}^{′}(c)=\frac{2}{3}.$*"] ["question-caea6f22-353c-51f3-b53e-c4874e2c30a8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/id #uuid "af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37"] ["answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer/id #uuid "61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e"] ["answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e" :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}"] ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/correct "answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e"] ["answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37" :answer-field/choices "answer-61ffeebf-caf7-5a1f-9fd2-b7d28409246e"] ["question-caea6f22-353c-51f3-b53e-c4874e2c30a8" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-af16ffc8-34d4-5d9f-9c83-e6de0ef51e37"] [17592186064160 :knowledge-point/questions "question-caea6f22-353c-51f3-b53e-c4874e2c30a8"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/id #uuid "93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/math-academy-id "q-166148"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/problem "Given that $f(2.1)=21,$ approximate ${f}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=2.1$ using a backward difference approximation.

{{field-1}}"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/worked-solution "We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=2.1.$ 

We choose the step size $h>0$ to be as small as possible. In this case, $h=0.1$ since the nearest backward point, for which we know the value of $f(x),$ is $f(2)=18$ (from the table above).

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2.1) & ≈\frac{f(2.1)-f(2.1-0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =10(f(2.1)-f(2)) \\  & =10(21-18) \\  & =10\cdot 3 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a" :answer-field/id #uuid "281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a"] ["answer-df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483" :answer/id #uuid "df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483"] ["answer-df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483" :answer/value "30"] ["answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a" :answer-field/correct "answer-df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483"] ["answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a" :answer-field/choices "answer-df2cbeda-e03c-506c-97d7-c7b56df4f483"] ["question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-281ee34a-5ec1-50ca-8410-459bfa2da35a"] [17592186092390 :knowledge-point/questions "question-93c6d227-1e4b-58a1-bf67-7c22cb760172"] ["question-fd542e6d-453b-52cc-8c0f-6c5dc531d308" :question/id #uuid "fd542e6d-453b-52cc-8c0f-6c5dc531d308"] ["question-fd542e6d-453b-52cc-8c0f-6c5dc531d308" :question/math-academy-id "q-166149"] ["question-fd542e6d-453b-52cc-8c0f-6c5dc531d308" :question/problem "Find the vertical asymptotes of $y=r(x),$ where $r(x)=\frac{3}{5x-2}.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-fd542e6d-453b-52cc-8c0f-6c5dc531d308" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that 

$$
y=r(x)=\frac{3}{5x-2}.
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. So, we find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to zero:

$$
5x-2=0\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{5}.

:question/problem "The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{Y}(y)=\frac{2}{3}y$ for $y\in [1,2]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-02ed11c8-435c-5d94-883f-47ba8fa464eb" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{3}y{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}y,\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [1,2].$

- Statement II is true. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4{x}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,1].$ So, when $x\in [0,1]$ and $y\in [1,2],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}={{(4{x}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{(\frac{2}{3}y)}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III""] ["question-02ed11c8-435c-5d94-883f-47ba8fa464eb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

$$

 
where $x\in [1,2].$ So, when $x\in [1,2]$ and $y\in [2,3],$ we obtain that 

$$

$$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is *not* true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

**Watch out!** It may seem counterintuitive that subtracting $k$ moves the graph to the right, while adding $k$ moves the graph to the left. However, this is in fact true.

To see why, let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below. Let's use this graph to plot the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

![](images/6c/6ca96bba855899f9b87ae06c166503c9af739fcd6bb2ec466a73b75cc70dde7f.png)

Let's take some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ and find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(x-2)$.

$$
f(3)=-4
$$

Then if

$$
x={\color{red}5}
$$

we have

$$
f(x-2) = f({\color{red}5}-2) = f(3) = -4
$$

which means that $({\color{red}5},-4)$ is on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ with the same $y$-value and a $x$-value that is $2$ units *greater*! Several more examples of points are shown below.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math] & Points on [math]y=f(x-2)[/math] \\ (3,-4) & (5,-4) \\ (1, 2) & (3, 2) \\ (0, 1.5) & (2, 1.5) \\ (-2, 0) & (0, 0)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's plot both curves.

![](images/ed/edae088984432dc7d0fff816a9e016ad221a3c897a78cf79efe6c784fa9176fe.png)

We see that every point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ is shifted $2$ units *to the right* of the corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x)$."]]}

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,1,-3⟩-⟨-7,5,2⟩ \\  & =⟨6,-4,-5⟩.\end{aligned}

and the plane $\Pi$ that is given by the equation 

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\langle 2 , 3 , 1 \rangle ) \cdot \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle = 0.
$$

 

First, note that $\mathbf{n} = \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle$ is a vector that's normal to the plane.

![](images/7b/7b2dfcd87c1f5e4e2c2b1a0b9a7f73899772e33e1020465b2b38d1b2de29a66c.png)

Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(2,3,1)$. Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,1⟩-⟨3,0,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,3,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The shortest distance $d$ from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane, as shown below.

![](images/26/26e494eef47db4dba3ac36dfa96c7e9a9d191321b22bb82874f3e74bbd7116ef.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 4+3\cdot 4+3\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4+12+6|}{\sqrt{16+16+4}} \\  & =\frac{|14|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is $\dfrac{7}{3}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "224c4104-9097-5a92-9c37-5d0fe22171a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3261 "8fc468d7-8c5a-51cb-a422-a6e8deebdd30" :question/math-academy-id "q-129166" :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,3,-6)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $-x+2y+2z=8.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-2$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2y+2z & =8 \\ -1(-2)+2(1)+2z & =8 \\ 2z & =4 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-2,1,2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,1,2⟩-⟨-2,3,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-1,2,2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|0\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot 2+8\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|0-4+16|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\  & =\frac{|12|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{12}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14537fa3-6b22-5ad7-8a11-c7c69ec06d24"} {:db/id 17592186476984 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262941 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "129b0757-3ac6-5753-b6e3-478a8023eb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186260037} {:answer/id #uuid "4de222b6-19ed-5d3c-a87c-f1b937df4849" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186260536} {:answer/id #uuid "65ac176a-0b06-5588-9781-22d9e0435725" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186260758} {:answer/id #uuid "816e3b5d-f9fa-5bd9-b29d-3f7e216e3a23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261004} {:answer/id #uuid "df122527-7c53-5616-83fd-4d0c7dd7847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261846}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260536} :answer-field/id #uuid "ffc75d90-c023-5fb9-a940-576505f511c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0498861d-e4e1-5581-aee5-353d6a78f4f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-129102" :question/problem "Given that $Q(4,-2,8)$ lies on the plane $Π:r\cdot ⟨-3,6,2⟩=-8$, find the shortest distance from $P(3,-4,2)$ to $Π.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find

From the equation of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-3,6,2⟩.$

\begin{aligned}-2x-3y+6z & =16 \\ -2(-2)-3(0)+6z & =16 \\ 6z & =12 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-2,0,2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,0,2⟩-⟨5,3,7⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,-3,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-7)\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+(-5)\cdot 6|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(6)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|14+9-30|}{\sqrt{4+9+36}} \\  & =\frac{|-7|}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{7}{7} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}14x+8y-8z & =-6 \\ 14(-1)+8(-2)-8z & =-6 \\ -8z & =24 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-1,-2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-2,-3⟩-⟨-11,-8,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,6,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨14,8,-8⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}14x+8y-8z & =-6 \\ 14(-1)+8(-2)-8z & =-6 \\ -8z & =24 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-1,-2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-2,-3⟩-⟨-11,-8,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,6,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨14,8,-8⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|10\cdot 14+6\cdot 8+1\cdot (-8)|}{\sqrt{(14)^{2}+{8}^{2}+(-8)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|140+48-8|}{\sqrt{196+64+64}} \\  & =\frac{|\,180\,|}{\sqrt{324}} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "96f5b1a1-014f-5d45-8c0e-94671204d88b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186493983}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00f6631c-af7b-53a2-83af-ac437e78d90b" :answer/type {:db/id "29956ecb-a28a-5406-b8dc-9776e9a3ccee" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Polynomial Raised to a Power Using the Chain Rule"}] :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = (3x^4+x^3)^5,$ calculate $\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f = g^5, \qquad g = 3x^4+x^3
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g}  = 5g^4,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x} = 12x^3 + 3x^2.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =5{g}^{4}\cdot (12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =5(3{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}{)}^{4}(12{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4{g}^{3},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-7.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (-7) \\  & =-28(1-7x)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317301 :question/id #uuid "f5911b4d-cb67-58a7-a1eb-0368289d94d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-342630"} {:db/id 17592186317308 :question/id #uuid :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2f0cdac9-57b2-5634-8d98-d6adf8a85204" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Function Using the Chain Rule"}] :question/problem "Given that $y = \sqrt{1-x^2},$ find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}.
$$

Here, we've used $u$ instead of $g$ for the intermediate variable. 

Let $u=1-x^2.$ Then $y = \sqrt u = u^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{2}u^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt u}
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}  = -2x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186097251 :question/id #uuid "854ec833-4bc0-54f0-9210-c708a9342fef" :question/math-academy-id "q-48730"} {:db/id 17592186097258 :question/id #uuid "ea97309c-a67a-5e7f-aa97-023276ac6669" :question/math-academy-id "q-48846"} {:db/id 17592186244040 :question/id #uuid "0ce97e32-c8a9-5155-bb70-6cb7385360f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-107291"} {:db/id 17592186244048 :question/id #uuid "c8b46779-d19f-5cca-987d-5f500a9de334" :question/math-academy-id "q-107360"} {:db/id 17592186297398 :question/id #uuid "2300bd8f-e3d1-544c-8ad1-127cb2f0bedc" :question/math-academy-id "q-314194"} {:db/id 17592186317312 :question/id #uuid "1f8a23e9-b484-592c-83ed-60ed3cc8b897" :question/math-academy-id "q-342680"} {:db/id 17592186317313 :question/id #uuid "c93d262c-d38e-53b1-ba9c-9af520b2e82c" :question/math-academy-id "q-342683"} {:db/id 17592186317321 :question/id #uuid "65a56fb3-c803-55e2-851b-d52f4cc805e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-342764" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096842 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2f0cdac9-57b2-5634-8d98-d6adf8a85204" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Function Using the Chain Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ea0b074e-9124-53da-b940-4a0beab23775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}}" :db/id 17592186316419}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ea0b074e-9124-53da-b940-4a0beab23775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}}" :db/id 17592186316419} :answer-field/id #uuid "cae0bf8f-009f-5cd9-a958-5250470d215a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186317025}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5x+1}}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=5x+1.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot 5 \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317326 :question/id #uuid "febc6c25-71ff-51d9-b851-6f19e65ebcd1" :question/math-academy-id "q-342802"} {:db/id 17592186520487 :question/id #uuid "98cde390-f268-5ffd-9f2f-31f016a0c432" :question/math-academy-id "q-107303" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "454a250f-2e0e-5eff-ad08-2e1a4569c3b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520091} {:answer/id #uuid "4cf36f6a-ac30-5d76-9499-88f79530ef58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520108} {:answer/id #uuid "a63c2527-a87a-5317-bb52-435b49980a68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520218} {:answer/id #uuid "ceae46e6-5020-51b1-a35e-422b64ddda99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520281} {:answer/id #uuid "edcc6c31-a212-5340-8bdb-e1b0f8c22746" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520341}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520091} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e463a5a-0bf7-5c15-8a84-e8fb513aab4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt{2x-1},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.\end{aligned}

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1108} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097750 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097807 :tutorial/content "Let's now prove the chain rule in the following form:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = f'(g(a)) \cdot g'(a)
$$

Let $f$ and $g$ be functions such that

- $g$ is differentiable at $a$,

- $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$.

Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $a$, and we compute its derivative as follows.

We start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a}
$$

Since $g$ is differentiable at $a$, it is also continuous there. Hence $g(x) \to g(a)$ as $x \to a$. For $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, we have $g(x) \ne g(a)$, so we may write

$$
\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a} 
= \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{g(x) - g(a)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}.
$$

Taking the limit as $x \to a$, and using the product rule for limits (which applies since both limits exist), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘g)^{'}(a) & ={lim}_{x\to a}(\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot \frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot {lim}_{x\to a}\frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a} \\  & ={f}^{'}(g(a))\cdot {g}^{'}(a)\end{aligned}
$$

as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "d34fc877-5572-53a2-b957-2c5d44a488f3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13330 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9ad2def5-511c-587f-9847-fa7af8e06405" :step/math-academy-id 466057} {:db/id 17592186097783 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097872 :tutorial/content "The **chain rule** for differentiation states that the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$ is given by

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

There is some intuition behind this rule: if we think of the derivatives as fractions, the ${\textrm{d}g}$'s would appear to cancel out.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\cancel{\text{d}g}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{d}g}}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

To see how the chain rule can be used to differentiate a function like 

$$
f(x) = (1+2x)^3,
$$

first, notice that the function can be written as a composite function

$$
f(g) = g^3, \qquad g(x) = 1+2x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}g}({g}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+2x) \\  & =3{g}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =6{g}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(x) = 1+2x$ for $g,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =6(1+2x)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We'll provide a derivation of the chain rule at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "743ad997-8732-5c0f-9676-ff1d44f3b513" :tutorial/math-academy-id 415 :tutorial/title "q-314207" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={({x}^{4}-3{x}^{3})}^{2},$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$

$)$" :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)={x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}$ and $f(g(x))=g(x)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{2})^{′}=2g, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{4}-3{x}^{3})^{′}=4{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule,

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

points $(1,-1)$ and $(4,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Perpendicular lines have slopes which are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,-1)$ and $(4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{1-(-1)}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{2}{3})=-1\,⇒\,m=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(-2,2).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-(-2)) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{3}{2}(x+2) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{3}{2}x-3 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}x-1\end{aligned}
$$

However, we want to write the equation in standard form. So, we will bring the $x$ term to the left-hand side and multiply both sides of the equation by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{2}x-1 \\ \frac{3}{2}x+y & =-1 \\ 2\cdot (\frac{3}{2}x+y) & =2\cdot (-1) \\ 3x+2y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186290470 :question/id #uuid "96f3c704-d5cd-55de-a550-62294d23b6d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-23631"} {:db/id 17592186290500 :question/id #uuid More precisely, we have the following theorem:

*If $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are mutually independent normal random variables such that*

$$
X_1 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim (\mu_2,\sigma_2^2), \qquad \ldots, \quad X_n\sim(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2),
$$

 

*and $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ are real constants, then the linear combination* 

$$
Y=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\ldots+a_nX_n
$$

 

*is normally distributed, where*

$$
Y\sim N(a_1\mu_1+a_2\mu_2+\ldots+a_n\mu_n, \: a_1^2\sigma_1^2+a_2^2\sigma_2^2+\ldots+a_n^2\sigma_n^2).
$$

$$
X_1\sim N({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}3}), \qquad X_2\sim  N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}4}), \qquad X_3\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}1})
$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y= \bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{3}X_1+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{2}X_2+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{4}X_3
$$

is normally distributed. 

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y.$ We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 2+2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1 \\  & =6+2+4 \\  & =12, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 3+4\cdot 4+16\cdot 1 \\  & =27+16+16 \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3} & ∼N(12,59).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It is vital that $X_1, X_2,\ldots X_n$ are *mutually independent*. $$

$$

 

*then the random variable* 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_n
$$

 

*is normally distributed, where*

$$
Y\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2+\ldots+\mu_n, \: \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\ldots+\sigma_n^2).
$$

$$

$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+X_3
$$

is normally distributed.

$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arcsch x) = -\dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+x^2}}.

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cotangent function is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arcoth x) = \dfrac{1}{1-x^2}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (0,1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the derivative of the base inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions, we can differentiate combinations of these functions, by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of

$$
y = \arsech{(-x^2)}
$$

Using the formulas above together with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡(-{x}^{2})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-{x}^{2})\sqrt{1-{(-{x}^{2})}^{2}}}\cdot {(-{x}^{2})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{-{x}^{2}\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Given that $f(x)=3e^x + \ln 3$, find $f'(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The derivative of $e^x$ is just $e^x$ itself. On the other hand, $\ln 3$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\eqalign{
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3e^x + \ln 3\right)\
                                                  &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( 3e^x\right) +  \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \ln 3 \right)\
                                                  &= 3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right) + 0\
                                                  &= 3 e^x.
}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186480049} {:db/id 17592186097160 :question/id #uuid "c5e514ba-2b59-510b-8545-fa3adc383ab3" :question/math-academy-id "q-1927"} {:db/id 17592186097316 :question/id #uuid Polynomial"}] :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=4e^x+ 3x^4 - x^2,$ find $f'(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\eqalign{ 
                          f'(x)             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x+3x^{4} - x^2 \right)\
                                             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x\right)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3x^{4}\right) -\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{2}\right) \
					     &= 4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right)+3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{4}\right) - 2x \			
                                             &=  4 e^x+  3 \cdot 4x^{3} - 2x \

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1\cdot {5}^{x}+2\cdot {2}^{x}-3x^2+1) \\ &=1\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({2}^{x})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x^2)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ &=1({5}^{x}\ln(5))+2({2}^{x}\ln(2))-3(2x)+0 \\ &=1\ln(5)\cdot {5}^{x}+2\ln(2)\cdot {2}^{x}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(-1)&=1\ln(5)\cdot {5}^{(-1)}+2\ln(2)\cdot {2}^{(-1)}-6(-1) \\ &=1(\frac{1}{5})\ln(5)+2(\frac{1}{2})\ln(2)-(6)(-1) \\ &=\frac{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}{5} + \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186479990 :question/id #uuid "df5079ea-2748-53c3-9b3e-39ecdb2bea5f"} {:db/id 17592186479993 :question/id #uuid "ec00e600-a612-5a76-94ca-79ecaa3d171e" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27addd41-1b34-5638-873b-b749efd9cbcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}(9)+2" :db/id 17592186479948}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186479948} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1395a30-edad-54d2-9382-c62a8875aa3f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186479991}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={9}^{x}-1{x}^{3}+2x-1$, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Applying the formula, we get

$$

$$

where $f(x) = e^x$.

Substituting the function $f(x)$ into the definition of $f'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x+h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot ({e}^{h}-1)}{h} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{h}-1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$
f'(x) = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1b006e01-04f6-5f6b-b435-b0f89163d7a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2613 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Rule for the Derivative of the Exponential Function"} :step/id #uuid "be9c264f-1e13-55c5-83f7-3217ce14b437" :step/math-academy-id 12311 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097749}} {:db/id 17592186097749 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097806 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the rule

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x,
$$

we begin with the definition of the derivative:

where $f(x) = e^x$.

Substituting the function $f(x)$ into the definition of $f'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x+h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot ({e}^{h}-1)}{h} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{h}-1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$
f'(x) = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1b006e01-04f6-5f6b-b435-b0f89163d7a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2613 :tutorial/title "Justifying the Rule for the Derivative of the Exponential Function"} :step/id #uuid "be9c264f-1e13-55c5-83f7-3217ce14b437" :step/math-academy-id 12311 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097749}} {:db/id 17592186097815 :tutorial/content "To derive the identity

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1\cdot {5}^{x}+2\cdot {2}^{x}-3x^2+1) \\ &=1\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({5}^{x})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({2}^{x})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x^2)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ &=1({5}^{x}\ln(5))+2({2}^{x}\ln(2))-3(2x)+0 \\ &=1\ln(5)\cdot {5}^{x}+2\ln(2)\cdot {2}^{x}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(-1)&=1\ln(5)\cdot {5}^{(-1)}+2\ln(2)\cdot {2}^{(-1)}-6(-1) \\ &=1(\frac{1}{5})\ln(5)+2(\frac{1}{2})\ln(2)-(6)(-1) \\ &=\frac{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}{5} + \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 6.\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{{field-2}}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2} &=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15})\frac{n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}
$$

Therefore, for ${b}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15} \\  & =\frac{n\pi }{15}\cdot \frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)} \\  & =\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221456 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221204 :question/id #uuid "3944f6e4-a3a8-5bad-87c5-18227ce223bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21858"} :knowledge-point/id $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+9({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms to find a common denominator:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(9-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\frac{36-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine coefficients:

$$
\frac{{b}_{n}(36-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}{4}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi (36-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi (36-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317448 :question/id #uuid "3f5c097d-b8ef-5e78-80f1-563c7c1e4885" :question/math-academy-id "q-343879"} {:db/id 17592186317449 :question/id #uuid series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-8(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)-(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))=1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)=1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=1 \\ {a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-1) &=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {a}_{n} &=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+1)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221457 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221206 :question/id #uuid "926606c2-1e1a-5aab-8f2e-826163a204a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-21875"} :knowledge-point/id 17592186317105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=0 \\ \pi B &=6\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317452 :question/id #uuid "de35c174-f52d-54b1-9320-5816b5069f2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-343905"} {:db/id 17592186317453 :question/id #uuid {y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A &=1 \\ 2\pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368351 :question/id #uuid "5d1812d8-39e4-5dd4-b731-c6eb976d76d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343896" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}):$

$$

$$

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A &=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049479} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27e72c91-6260-57d4-8f2b-d360cd74d1b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value :topic/math-academy-id 6386} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222397 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222522 :tutorial/content "Suppose a linear ODE has a periodic forcing term whose Fourier series is known, for example

$$
y' + ky = f(x),
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
f(x) \sim \frac{c_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(c_n\cos(\omega_n x) + d_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

A standard strategy is to look for a *particular* solution with the *same Fourier frequencies*:

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big)
$$

Then, the method includes the following steps:

- **Step 1:** Differentiate term-by-term.

Using $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\cos(\omega_n x)=-\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x)$ and $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\sin(\omega_n x)=\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)$, we get

$$
y_p' \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(-a_n\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x) + b_n\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

- **Step 2:** Substitute into the ODE and collect like terms

Then, we plug $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the equation, and rewrite the left-hand side as

$$
\Big(\substack{\large\text{free} \[3pt] \large\text{term}}\Big) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{cosine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \cos(\omega_n x) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{sine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \sin(\omega_n x).
$$

- **Step 3:** Equate coefficients.

Because the Fourier series representation is unique (up to convergence issues we ignore here), we match:

- the free terms, and

- for each $n\ge 1$, the cosine coefficients and sine coefficients.

This produces:

- one equation for $a_0$ (from the constant term), and

- a $2\times 2$ linear system for $(a_n,b_n)$ for each $n\ge 1$.

- **Step 4:** Write the Fourier series of $y_p.$

After solving for $a_0$, $a_n$, and $b_n$, substitute them back into

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "84328521-7170-5404-8ec2-a41475c2ad15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14711 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0521dca3-2fe6-50aa-8dc9-282e35ffe718" :step/math-academy-id 607546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222398}} {:db/id 17592186222398 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221455 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221203 :question/id #uuid "03fbfe2c-b12f-5220-9fae-e0dfe210a505" :question/math-academy-id "e-21857"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4733fab7-18ca-5336-9aba-53212ddbf87b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186050010}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222031} {:db/id 17592186222032} {:db/id 17592186317443} {:db/id 17592186397662} {:db/id 17592186397676} {:db/id 17592186512930}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving First Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function"} :step/id #uuid "ab947003-2e2f-5620-996d-e8070699c2a1" :step/math-academy-id 607547 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222399}} {:db/id 17592186222399 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222523 :tutorial/content "For second-order linear ODEs, the overall algorithm is the same as for first-order equations: 

- we assume a Fourier series for $y_p$,

- substitute into the ODE, and

- match coefficients.

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form 

$$
y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)
$$

with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified.

The key insight comes from the fact that the differential operator 

$$
L[y] = y'' + \omega^2 y
$$

maps cosines to cosines and sines to sines. This means we can match the form of our assumed solution $y_p$ to the form of the forcing function $f(x),$ which saves a great deal of work.

This leads to some powerful shortcuts:

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure cosine series* (an even function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure cosine series (all $b_n=0$).

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure sine series* (an odd function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure sine series (all $a_n=0$, including $a_0=0$).

- If the constant term in the series for $f(x)$ is zero, the constant term in $y_p$ will also be zero (so $a_0=0$).

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "12f51f58-a298-5fc1-9540-6d9f4611481b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14712 :tutorial/title "Second Order ODEs With Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "d1b21edf-14d7-5094-a313-f622ad12149b" :step/math-academy-id 607550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222403}} {:db/id 17592186222400 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221456 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221204 :question/id #uuid "3944f6e4-a3a8-5bad-87c5-18227ce223bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21858"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5e39d476-7dcb-5213-a461-df7bd1919b9f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050378}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222035} {:db/id 17592186222037} {:db/id 17592186317447} {:db/id 17592186317448} {:db/id 17592186317449} {:db/id 17592186317450} {:db/id 17592186368331} {:db/id 17592186368337} {:db/id 17592186484247} {:db/id 17592186484267} {:db/id 17592186507450} {:db/id 17592186507482} {:db/id 17592186512900}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Second Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function"} :step/id #uuid "2fb61d84-6e73-5592-aa15-0582c4b7b2f2" :step/math-academy-id 607551 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222401}} {:db/id 17592186222401 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222528 :tutorial/content "A forcing harmonic can cause *resonance* when its frequency matches the natural frequency of the homogeneous equation.

In cases like that, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1:** Find the natural frequency.

For an equation of the form

$$
y''+\omega^2 y = f(x),
$$

the homogeneous solution oscillates with natural frequency $\omega$.

- **Step 2:** Find the forcing frequencies.

If $f$ is $2L$-periodic, then its Fourier series uses harmonics

$$
\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),\qquad \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),
$$

whose frequencies are

$$
\omega_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}\qquad(n\ge 1).
$$

A harmonic is *resonant* exactly when $\omega_n=\omega$.

- **Step 3:** Form the particular solution ansatz for each harmonic.

- For a *non-resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n\ne \omega$), we use the standard ansatz:

$$
y_{p_n}=A\cos(\omega_n x)+B\sin(\omega_n x)
$$

- For a *resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n=\omega$), this form overlaps with the homogeneous solution. We must use the *modified ansatz* by multiplying by $x{:}$

$$
y_{p_n}=x\left(A\cos(\omega x)+B\sin(\omega x)\right)
$$

This extra factor of $x$ produces a new trial function that can match the forcing term.

When $f$ is given as a Fourier series, we check each harmonic:

- *non-resonant* harmonics contribute ordinary sine/cosine terms to $y_p,$ while

- *resonant* harmonics contribute terms multiplied by $x.$

In particular, the resonant harmonic is the one with index $n$ satisfying

$$
\frac{n\pi}{L}=\omega.
$$

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Because $f$ has no free term and is a pure cosine series, we assume

$$
y_p \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $y''_p$ and $y_p$ into the equation and have

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty -a_n n^2\pi^2\cos(n\pi x)
-
4\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x)\right)
=
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty -a_n(n^2\pi^2+4)\cos(n\pi x)
=
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain

$$
-a_n(n^2\pi^2+4)=\dfrac{2}{n^2}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
a_n=-\dfrac{2}{n^2(n^2\pi^2+4)}.
$$

Therefore, a Fourier series for a particular solution is

$$
y_p \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \: -\dfrac{2}{n^2(n^2\pi^2+4)} \cdot \cos(n\pi x).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f2d6d8f9-00d1-552b-889a-e54ed8d22d21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14873 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of Solving a Second Order ODE"} :step/id #uuid "483f5b2d-f9cb-5272-a15f-759e449ff9c0" :step/math-academy-id 607559 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222400}}] :activity/title "Solving ODEs Using Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221475} {:db/id 17592186222397 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222522 :tutorial/content "Suppose a linear ODE has a periodic forcing term whose Fourier series is known, for example

$$
y' + ky = f(x),
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
f(x) \sim \frac{c_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(c_n\cos(\omega_n x) + d_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

A standard strategy is to look for a *particular* solution with the *same Fourier frequencies*:

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big)
$$

Then, the method includes the following steps:

- **Step 1:** Differentiate term-by-term.

Using $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\cos(\omega_n x)=-\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x)$ and $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\sin(\omega_n x)=\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)$, we get

$$
y_p' \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(-a_n\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x) + b_n\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

- **Step 2:** Substitute into the ODE and collect like terms

Then, we plug $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the equation, and rewrite the left-hand side as

$$
\Big(\substack{\large\text{free} \[3pt] \large\text{term}}\Big) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{cosine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \cos(\omega_n x) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{sine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \sin(\omega_n x).
$$

- **Step 3:** Equate coefficients.

Because the Fourier series representation is unique (up to convergence issues we ignore here), we match:

- the free terms, and

- for each $n\ge 1$, the cosine coefficients and sine coefficients.

This produces:

- one equation for $a_0$ (from the constant term), and

- a $2\times 2$ linear system for $(a_n,b_n)$ for each $n\ge 1$.

- **Step 4:** Write the Fourier series of $y_p.$

After solving for $a_0$, $a_n$, and $b_n$, substitute them back into

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "84328521-7170-5404-8ec2-a41475c2ad15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14711 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0521dca3-2fe6-50aa-8dc9-282e35ffe718" :step/math-academy-id 607546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222398}} {:db/id 17592186222522 :tutorial/content "Suppose a linear ODE has a periodic forcing term whose Fourier series is known, for example

- we assume a Fourier series for $y_p$,

- substitute into the ODE, and

- match coefficients.

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form 

$$
y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)
$$

with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified.

The key insight comes from the fact that the differential operator 

$$
L[y] = y'' + \omega^2 y
$$

maps cosines to cosines and sines to sines. This means we can match the form of our assumed solution $y_p$ to the form of the forcing function $f(x),$ which saves a great deal of work.

This leads to some powerful shortcuts:

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure cosine series* (an even function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure cosine series (all $b_n=0$).

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure sine series* (an odd function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure sine series (all $a_n=0$, including $a_0=0$).

- If the constant term in the series for $f(x)$ is zero, the constant term in $y_p$ will also be zero (so $a_0=0$).

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "12f51f58-a298-5fc1-9540-6d9f4611481b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14712 :tutorial/title "Second Order ODEs With Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "d1b21edf-14d7-5094-a313-f622ad12149b" :step/math-academy-id 607550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222403}} {:db/id 17592186222523 :tutorial/content "For second-order linear ODEs, the overall algorithm is the same as for first-order equations:

In cases like that, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1:** Find the natural frequency.

For an equation of the form

$$
y''+\omega^2 y = f(x),
$$

the homogeneous solution oscillates with natural frequency $\omega$.

- **Step 2:** Find the forcing frequencies.

If $f$ is $2L$-periodic, then its Fourier series uses harmonics

$$
\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),\qquad \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),
$$

whose frequencies are

$$
\omega_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}\qquad(n\ge 1).
$$

A harmonic is *resonant* exactly when $\omega_n=\omega$.

- **Step 3:** Form the particular solution ansatz for each harmonic.

- For a *non-resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n\ne \omega$), we use the standard ansatz:

$$
y_{p_n}=A\cos(\omega_n x)+B\sin(\omega_n x)
$$

- For a *resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n=\omega$), this form overlaps with the homogeneous solution. We must use the *modified ansatz* by multiplying by $x{:}$

$$
y_{p_n}=x\left(A\cos(\omega x)+B\sin(\omega x)\right)
$$

This extra factor of $x$ produces a new trial function that can match the forcing term.

When $f$ is given as a Fourier series, we check each harmonic:

- *non-resonant* harmonics contribute ordinary sine/cosine terms to $y_p,$ while

- *resonant* harmonics contribute terms multiplied by $x.$

In particular, the resonant harmonic is the one with index $n$ satisfying

$$
\frac{n\pi}{L}=\omega.
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "1aff3ba6-cd76-5ae7-bcd6-d05e9fb44694" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14776 :tutorial/title "Cases Where the Forcing Term Induces Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "6d7e21fe-4716-5031-8d15-1ac9a8196ed5" :step/math-academy-id 607555 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222402}} {:db/id 17592186222528 :tutorial/content "A forcing harmonic can cause *resonance* when its frequency matches the natural frequency of the homogeneous equation.

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f7afbc4a-cfc0-549a-b6ce-77b93f2927bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-343907" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A &=1 \\ 2\pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3730dcd9-f2ec-50da-be0d-14c755f56a78"} {:db/id 17592186484349 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484247 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01560cae-7dae-59d2-abe1-84a1d7d6c454" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186483571} {:answer/id #uuid "4acd6ba8-bd4d-5211-b24b-b92da18d82bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186483701} {:answer/id #uuid "88c5fee9-6d57-52b7-8a9a-fc2fb915b829" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186483848} {:answer/id #uuid "c8a5f1d7-c219-529e-8a3d-b15c3dd5908b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{n(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186483962}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186483571} :answer-field/id #uuid "1af9059e-73b7-5797-a59d-c6b481acd050" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186484095}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "88bf7711-bb0b-51a9-9d4e-44874b161912" :question/math-academy-id "q-343878" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$

$$
