The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+36({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms to find a common denominator:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(36-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(\frac{324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients:

$$
\frac{{a}_{n}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}{9}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c1f72d93-f5f8-5ed4-a7c5-2788d86bcace" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484356}} {:db/id 17592186484354 :step/content {:db/id 17592186397690 :question/answer-fields {y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{36{\pi }^{2}}=6\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $1$-periodic function $(L=\frac{1}{2})$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{(\frac{1}{2})}=2n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=6\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))+x(-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x):$

$$
[-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-12\pi A &=0 \\ 12\pi B &=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{108\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{108\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d16e1bd2-5d3a-57fc-8ce5-5535cc365650" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484314}} {:db/id 17592186484356 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317450 :question/answer-fields The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-8(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=8 \\ {b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8) &=\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {b}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e1c91699-1134-58dc-ab5b-ea077a7ce0b0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484354}} {:db/id 17592186484357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484267 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2cf7e913-fe58-5754-9149-b09245f9b60a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/id 17592186483642} {:answer/id #uuid "53e18eaf-8bd1-5628-92d7-801bfaf1946a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/id 17592186483717} {:answer/id #uuid "6175ce1f-2050-5a57-bf7b-da70f7498dcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/id 17592186483754} {:answer/id #uuid "b701f81d-8ac2-5b72-b41d-29bb579466f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{16}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/id 17592186483935}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186483642} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe77b4de-90c9-5d84-bcb6-651adb4b6345" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186484192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b49a66f8-383d-5ed3-a1a9-b2f05fd8c09d" :question/math-academy-id "q-343873" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-16y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A &=1 \\ 2\pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6d225572-fd74-5350-9e69-efe599d6dfa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-343883" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-8y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-8(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=8 \\ {b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8) &=\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {b}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e1c91699-1134-58dc-ab5b-ea077a7ce0b0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484354}} {:db/id 17592186484354 :step/content {:db/id 17592186397690 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d694cb78-fd17-5d72-bd5e-fb91875a20a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343891" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $1$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{36{\pi }^{2}}=6\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $1$-periodic function $(L=\frac{1}{2})$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{(\frac{1}{2})}=2n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=6\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))+x(-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x):$

$$
[-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-12\pi A &=0 \\ 12\pi B &=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{108\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{108\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d16e1bd2-5d3a-57fc-8ce5-5535cc365650" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484314}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26abab5a-e0d3-5a63-b7b9-8c8b067c042b" :answer/type {:db/id $$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=4 \\ \pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{4}{\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{4x}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e364e0b-e003-503e-aadb-895d96ad9926" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507557}} {:db/id 17592186507540 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507450 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d7f8754-41a4-514c-86d1-d5647b54333b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{98\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186506703} {:answer/id #uuid "a564bbb9-af52-596a-bcf1-bb101438423e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507039} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e53c4f-ca05-5e48-9e4b-fba6af34790c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507136} {:answer/id #uuid "e6ebfba2-6c04-5678-a8f3-079e02b2c158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{n(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}" :db/id 17592186507185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507136} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8a63a77-7e75-5948-b4a4-f7660df42d29" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186507393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "776f8284-bdba-5ab6-8f5c-16f7e1be5e32" :question/math-academy-id "q-343877" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+49y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+49({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))+x(-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))\end{aligned}

$$
[-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\pi A &=0 \\ 6\pi B &=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{54\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{54\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x).

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-4({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine coefficients, we obtain 

$$

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}

$$
{y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{9{\pi }^{2}}=3\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=3\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))+x(-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x):$

$$

$$

$$
-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$

$$

\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2} &=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n} &=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15})\frac{n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}
$$

Therefore, for ${b}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15} \\  & =\frac{n\pi }{15}\cdot \frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)} \\  & =\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).

$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$

$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5d1812d8-39e4-5dd4-b731-c6eb976d76d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343896" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}):$

$$
[-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\pi }{3}A &=0 \\ \frac{2\pi }{3}B &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{3}{2\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})-6(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))=6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).

$$

$$

$$

$$

17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2+6x-3y+xy$ on the closed region $D$ enclosed by $y=2{x}^{2}$ and $y=8.$ You are given that $f$ has a critical point at $(3,-6),$ and on the boundary of the region the points that could give rise to extreme values are $(-2,8),$ $(1,2),$ and $(2,8).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

**Step 1.** Find the critical points inside the region $D.$ 

To determine the critical points, let's first sketch the region:

![](images/06/06660df896e67cef560398ca24217cdba2e2b9a34fe40f1829b3e1d5d2db24e3.png)

Since the critical point $(3,-6)$ does not lie inside $D,$ we do not include that point in the list of candidates for the extrema.

$$

$$

17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(2,0)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(2,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+4 \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4 \\  & =13-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (13-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 12\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution $t=\pi \in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\pi .$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain two candidate points:

$$
(3,0),\,(-3,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,0) & =(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(2)+4 \\  & =4+0-8+4 \\  & =0 \\ f(3,0) & =(3)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(3)+4 \\  & =9+0-12+4 \\  & =1 \\ f(-3,0) & =(-3)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(-3)+4 \\  & =9+0+12+4 \\  & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(2,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $25$ at the point $(-3,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186125064 :question/id #uuid "784d8995-a39a-5567-b522-960291c7a1e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-37372"} {:db/id 17592186351509 :question/id #uuid "8a46a5d2-f50e-55ed-a8fd-136bbe52d472" :question/math-academy-id "q-83442" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b85fe54-e88e-50e7-a167-e5f47c6caf9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=2$" :db/id 17592186348681} {:answer/id #uuid "ae644282-0673-52d6-b565-29bff873652c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=1$ and ${f}_{max}=2$" :db/id 17592186349988} {:answer/id #uuid "decd099b-7990-5e6c-9d38-3fb5e4b3f69e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=0$ and ${f}_{max}=2$" :db/id 17592186350394} {:answer/id #uuid "e42eeb73-b5de-5a01-9ca0-dedfb055c39f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=0$ and ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186350449} {:answer/id #uuid "f978cd4e-a6f5-5a68-8a84-167294111486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186350639}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350394} :answer-field/id #uuid "ccbb50fc-642e-575f-bc5f-9e1b642c347e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351064}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+1$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(0,0)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ This gives  

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t+1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1)^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives the solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points: 

$$
(1,0),\,(0,1),\,(-1,0),\,(0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =(0)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-0+1 \\  & =1 \\ f(1,0) & =(1)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =1-0+1 \\  & =2 \\ f(0,1) & =(0)^{2}-(1)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-1+1 \\  & =0 \\ f(-1,0) & =(-1)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =1-0+1 \\  & =2 \\ f(0,-1) & =(0)^{2}-(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-1+1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and  $(0,1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $2$ at the point $(-1,0),$ and $(1,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186354504 :question/id #uuid "6872646b-2fa0-5569-8460-8a72ff9bd7ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-86723" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8dfe7cc3-7e1e-531b-9679-17d6282f66cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-7$ and ${f}_{max}=-1$" :db/id 17592186352805} {:answer/id #uuid "9480fe29-ef08-57e8-a109-77655e61781e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-2$ and ${f}_{max}=7$" :db/id 17592186352855} {:answer/id #uuid "959a80c9-8d6f-5ebf-854d-92e4451dd1a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-2$ and ${f}_{max}=-1$" :db/id 17592186352863} {:answer/id #uuid "d4beecad-5b8a-50ab-b3aa-c19725a94642" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=2$ and ${f}_{max}=7$" :db/id 17592186353411} {:answer/id #uuid "e95fd2c0-5b91-5181-bf86-2c14f39b7349" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=7$" :db/id 17592186353598}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186352855} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b1b2db2-672f-587c-8384-08bd0b27587d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186353887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x-1$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(1,0)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(1,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}-2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-1 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =3-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution $t=\pi \in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\pi .$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain two candidate points:

$$
(2,0),\,(-2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & =(1)^{2}+(0)^{2}-2(1)-1 \\  & =1+0-2-1 \\  & =-2 \\ f(2,0) & =(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-2(2)-1 \\  & =4+0-4-1 \\  & =-1 \\ f(-2,0) & =(-2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-2(-2)-1 \\  & =4+0+4-1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-2$ at the point $(1,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $7$ at the point $(-2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186363541 :question/id #uuid "48e27a98-5e9a-5abd-8c04-d1e75ddfe8ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-167162" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a620cea-c724-5cd1-81af-543f3d2c51dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-\sqrt{3}$ and ${f}_{max}=\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363543} {:answer/id #uuid "2e0d1a43-6f8b-5644-93e8-16948f17dafa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=3-2\sqrt{3}$ and ${f}_{max}=3+2\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363544} {:answer/id #uuid "81a5b1aa-671f-52ad-9681-35461c2b2509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=3+2\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363545} {:answer/id #uuid "ddc0f0b2-6ebe-53e9-96ad-e380f02b0b9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=3$" :db/id 17592186363546} {:answer/id #uuid "eb7e87b5-ff70-5a36-ac7c-77dc99ac2caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=0$ and ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186363547}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363545} :answer-field/id #uuid "ab3adac3-45ef-501d-ba44-cfa5be5274bd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363542}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2y$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(0,-1)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,-1)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives two solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain three candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{3},0),\,(0,-\sqrt{3}),\,(0,\sqrt{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3},0) & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+2(0) \\  & =3+0+0 \\  & =3 \\ f(0,-\sqrt{3}) & =(0)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3-2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3-2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,\sqrt{3}) & ={0}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3+2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =0+1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $3+2\sqrt{3}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186401579 :question/id #uuid "e7d00266-1ded-5f4c-819a-7467528496c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-167165" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186401580}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-2x,\,2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x &=0 \\ 2y &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 32\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:

$$
(4,0),\,(0,4),\,(-4,0),\,(0,-4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and $(-4,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $17$ at the points $(0,4)$ and $(0,-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186404364 :question/id #uuid "8392959c-a393-5152-9307-9f96b5859277" :question/math-academy-id "q-86722" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "233ac657-1b6c-5153-ae47-c73f6a18839b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-8$ and ${f}_{max}=10$" :db/id 17592186404366} {:answer/id #uuid "1398af4c-7ac7-570a-a8f9-3e7b4fb50230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=1$ and ${f}_{max}=10$" :db/id 17592186404367} {:answer/id #uuid "9e7069d6-ca3e-5408-8724-9f786c398052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=10$" :db/id 17592186404368} {:answer/id #uuid "ff9e5045-1ffc-5c1d-8753-b170299e5ae5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-8$ and ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186404369} {:answer/id #uuid "015fd256-8e43-5c2a-9c03-aa641f0627f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-8$ and ${f}_{max}=8$" :db/id 17592186404370}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404366} :answer-field/id #uuid "20a29c76-a92d-5a15-9982-689804fc2dba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404365}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-4xy$ on the closed elliptical region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\le 9}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$  

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To do that, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-4y,\,-4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-4y &=0 \\ -4x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-18\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\ -18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate points:

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+2$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(1,0)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(1,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}-4(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+2 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (4{cos}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6)^{′} & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0 \\ 8\operatorname{sin}⁡t(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives the solution $t=\pi \in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\pi .$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain two candidate points:

$$
(2,0),\,(-2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & =2(1)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(1)+2 \\  & =2+0-4+2 \\  & =0 \\ f(-2,0) & =2(-2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(-2)+2 \\  & =8+0+8+2 \\  & =18 \\ f(2,0) & =2(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(2)+2 \\  & =8+0-8+2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(1,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $18$ at the point $(-2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186446482 :question/id #uuid "49397200-f106-5784-934d-a685f0e1e2bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-83436"} {:db/id function has no critical points." :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

Since f has no critical points in D , the list of candidates for the extrema won't contain critical points.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ \frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\le 1$, this equation gives the solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval,  $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,$ and $\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain candidate points: 

$$
(\frac{1}{2},0),\,(0,1),\,(0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ f(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+1 \\  & =1 \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the point $(0,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186446489 :question/id #uuid "e78c82da-b48f-5dab-aeb6-fcde924129f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-83438"} {:db/id "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** 

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b8b379fb-f7e4-5cdb-b25a-69a6c2ae9cf2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7879 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} ![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b8b379fb-f7e4-5cdb-b25a-69a6c2ae9cf2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7879 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ This gives  

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t+1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1)^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives the solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points: 

$$
(1,0),\,(0,1),\,(-1,0),\,(0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =(0)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-0+1 \\  & =1 \\ f(1,0) & =(1)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =1-0+1 \\  & =2 \\ f(0,1) & =(0)^{2}-(1)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-1+1 \\  & =0 \\ f(-1,0) & =(-1)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =1-0+1 \\  & =2 \\ f(0,-1) & =(0)^{2}-(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =0-1+1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and  $(0,1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $2$ at the point $(-1,0),$ and $(1,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "33ee7691-7413-57d9-a695-13ab29e0b850" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500384}} {:db/id 17592186500415 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284576 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3bbbdac6-b001-5c5f-a60f-08cd76657100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186282212} {:answer/id #uuid "53ba36d0-f558-562c-accf-8fca00ae7e4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186282403} {:answer/id #uuid "63258b6f-64b9-5b0d-a947-8f6914ff9da5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186282542} {:answer/id #uuid "cf9a08c9-cc69-53e4-a5f5-c418f62f71ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186283499} {:answer/id #uuid "fa92ffe0-5aae-5f21-b93c-77bdca986153" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186283879}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283499} :answer-field/id #uuid "f2315c40-ba66-5f86-acdd-4cc57b9568cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284366}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ddfa127f-a279-50f9-9daa-00b98d8bc9d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-167160" :question/problem "Find the global maximum of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-{y}^{2}+2y-1$ on the closed square $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1\}.$ You're given that $f$ has a critical point at $(0,1),$ and on the boundary of the square the points that could give rise to extreme values are the vertices." :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

**Step 2.** Find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values. 

In this case, we are *given* the points on the boundary of our region that could potentially be global extrema for $f.$ These are

$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & ={1}^{3}-{0}^{2}+2(0)-1 \\  & =1-0+0-1 \\  & =0 \\ f(1,1) & ={1}^{3}-{1}^{2}+2(1)-1 \\  & =1-1+2-1 \\  & =1 \\ f(0,1) & ={0}^{3}-{1}^{2}+2(1)-1 \\  & =0-1+2-1 \\  & =0 \\ f(0,0) & ={0}^{3}-{0}^{2}+2(0)-1 \\  & =0-0+0-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,-1)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives two solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain three candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{3},0),\,(0,-\sqrt{3}),\,(0,\sqrt{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3},0) & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+2(0) \\  & =3+0+0 \\  & =3 \\ f(0,-\sqrt{3}) & =(0)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3-2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3-2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,\sqrt{3}) & ={0}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3+2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =0+1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To do that, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-4y,\,-4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-4y &=0 \\ -4x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-18\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\ -18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate points:

$$
(3,0),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(3,0)$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-8$ | $10$ | $-8$ | $10$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-8$ at the points $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $10$ at the points $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}).$"} :step/id #uuid "17b3d78a-4c11-56d5-8c1a-c9703c363db5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519611}} {:db/id 17592186519620 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125033 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f08487e-af26-5c1f-962f-ed237732c2fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=4$ and ${f}_{max}=6$" :db/id 17592186446405} {:answer/id #uuid "0f5adf40-0426-5a10-8817-dc97f008412e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-50$ and ${f}_{max}=20$" :db/id 17592186446406} {:answer/id #uuid "95dff366-2d95-5d09-afa0-223b43913ab4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-50$ and ${f}_{max}=4$" :db/id 17592186446440} {:answer/id #uuid "e08526c7-85a2-54ab-b8bb-bc02be965b47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-50$ and ${f}_{max}=6$" :db/id 17592186446459} {:answer/id #uuid "f5d065ac-c348-5dd1-a57c-c5e5b0070028" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-20$ and ${f}_{max}=20$" :db/id 17592186446464}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186446459} :answer-field/id #uuid "78b2ba2b-f79b-5ccd-88fe-1d78549d2f08" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122798}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fc6c7d4b-ed06-5426-80f2-415a147181e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37149" :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2+6x-3y+xy$ on the closed region $D$ enclosed by $y=2{x}^{2}$ and $y=8.$ You are given that $f$ has a critical point at $(3,-6),$ and on the boundary of the region the points that could give rise to extreme values are $(-2,8),$ $(1,2),$ and $(2,8).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$
