elliptical region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\le 9}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$  

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To do that, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-4y,\,-4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-4y &=0 \\ -4x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-18\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\ -18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate points:

$$
(3,0),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(3,0)$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-8$ | $10$ | $-8$ | $10$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-8$ at the points $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $10$ at the points $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}).$"} :step/id #uuid What is the probability that a randomly chosen program lasts less than $30$ minutes?" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the duration of the radio program. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U[27,34]$, and we wish to compute $P(X < 30)$.

In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$, then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{\frac{1}{b - a},\begin{vmatrix}a \le x \le b \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U[27,34]$, we have the following probability density function:

$$
{\frac{1}{7},\begin{vmatrix}27 \le x \le 34 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X < 30) &= \int_{27}^{30}f(x)dx \\
&= \int_{27}^{30}\frac{1}{7}dx \\
&= \left.\frac{x}{7}\right|_{27}^{30} \\
&= \frac{30}{7} - \frac{27}{7} \\
&= \frac{3}{7}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049239} {:db/id 17592186158001 :question/id #uuid "42f3bd3c-7b50-5148-a250-433188b50554" :question/math-academy-id "q-94876"} {:db/id 17592186158007 :question/id #uuid "fcb100e3-d695-54a0-a6a7-768dc5fef8fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-96733"} {:db/id 17592186157376 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157196 :question/id #uuid "70b91fcc-70a7-580d-84b0-b24a7e2643d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8306"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "38f8d9f6-9ef8-5cc1-b2d8-38936c08468a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048513}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186158002 :question/id #uuid "a2bf66f0-fdce-5219-924b-0a53cc32c2d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94877"} {:db/id 17592186158008 :question/id #uuid "783a0029-9876-5d5f-8e19-0749f3f99743" :question/math-academy-id "q-96910"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Expected Value in Context"} {:db/id 17592186157196 :question/id #uuid "70b91fcc-70a7-580d-84b0-b24a7e2643d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8306" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186157376 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "38f8d9f6-9ef8-5cc1-b2d8-38936c08468a" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Expected Value in Context"}] :question/problem "A video game randomly generates an obstacle the player has to avoid. What is the mean $x$-coordinate of the obstacle?" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the $x$-coordinate of a randomly generated obstacle. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U[-6,12]$, and we wish to compute $\textrm E[X]$.

In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$, then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U[-6,12]$, we have the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{-6+12}{2} = 3
$$

If the visiting time is uniformly distributed, what is its variance?" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the visiting time of a randomly chosen visitor. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U[1.5,4.5]$, and we wish to compute $\textrm{Var}[X]$.

In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$, then $X$ has the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U[1.5,4.5]$, we have the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{(4.5-1.5)^2}{12} = \dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}
$$

Therefore, the variance is

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}\,\textrm{hr}^2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186158003 :question/id #uuid "590a2520-a7d3-5b41-9ce1-0410853f55f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-94879"} {:db/id 17592186158009 :question/id #uuid "b16fcf14-b902-58e8-beb4-6f1dfce4ba1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-96923" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186157377 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "610bddb6-0731-53d1-9fcf-ab202d4cf151" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Variance in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "939ab6aa-46ef-5b62-9709-d520ce550ff6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4}{13}hr^{2}" :db/id 17592186156976} {:answer/id #uuid "de1db298-9864-523f-a190-3914fffd534e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}hr^{2}" :db/id 17592186156977} {:answer/id #uuid "e39c129d-f3c3-5dd6-b602-51bf0cabbf11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}hr^{2}" :db/id 17592186156978} {:answer/id #uuid "0396c0de-bf26-58e9-a966-a93f40bbc719" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{11}{4}hr^{2}" :db/id 17592186156979} {:answer/id #uuid "6a867ee1-e1b2-5c08-b448-a7cabe81ef09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}hr^{2}" :db/id 17592186156980}] :answer-field/id #uuid "5dcb98ae-1119-51fd-82e9-711264df4277" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186156975}] :question/problem "The time it takes a mechanic to repair a car is uniformly distributed with a minimum of $2$ hours and a maximum of $6$ hours. {:db/id 17592186158262}} {:db/id 17592186158261 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158542 :tutorial/content "In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$ is uniformly distributed, then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{\frac{1}{b - a},\begin{vmatrix}a \le x \le b \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution:

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{\frac{1}{8},\begin{vmatrix}6 \le x \le 14 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \ge 9) &= \int_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}dx \\
&= \frac{1}{8}\int_{9}^{14}dx \\
&= \frac{1}{8}[x]_{9}^{14} \\
&= \frac{1}{8}[14 - 9] \\
&= \frac{5}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= \frac{a + b}{2} \\
&= \frac{6 + 14}{2} \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

17592186372792}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

Let $F(x)=4{x}^{2}-6x+3$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-6x+3$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(4{x}^{2}-6x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+3x]}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((\frac{4}{3}\cdot {3}^{3}-3\cdot {3}^{2}+3\cdot 3)-(\frac{4}{3}\cdot (-3)^{3}-3\cdot (-3)^{2}+3\cdot (-3))) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(18-(-72)) \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372794 :question/id #uuid "e2e5c8de-82af-59f7-9831-0d0c36257889" :question/math-academy-id "q-341792"} {:db/id 17592186372797 :question/id #uuid "0b41ae3b-0d3e-5b1e-a78c-fa1ec34fc5b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-341794" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221444 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cb301102-1a82-5a81-bb11-b9fc56cd1dc7" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Constant Term For the Fourier Series"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4377e0c6-ff5d-58c7-b0be-e00480e92ef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186372799}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4377e0c6-ff5d-58c7-b0be-e00480e92ef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186372799} :answer-field/id #uuid "5b7b647f-bcd2-53cf-8319-b5595a4ddf84" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186372798}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

(instead of $2\pi$), the "usual" Fourier formulas still work, but the sine and cosine inputs must be rescaled so that each term completes an integer number of oscillations over one period. 

We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "5bb98db0-8e34-5cf2-8911-56a6971740ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14681 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

I. $(5x^2-10x^3) \div (5x)$

II. $(1-x^3) \div (x^3)$

III. $(2x^5) \cdot (-x^3-7)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression I is a polynomial. Even though polynomials are *not* closed under division, the quotient of these two polynomials results in a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3})÷(5x) & =\frac{5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3}}{5x} \\  & =\frac{5x(x-2{x}^{2})}{5x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{5x}(x-2{x}^{2})}{\cancel{5x}} \\  & =x-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Expression II is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

- Expression III is a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186048180} {:db/id 17592186048957} {:db/id 17592186049500} {:db/id 17592186050323} {:db/id 17592186050827} {:db/id 17592186092553 :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Operations on Polynomials"}] :question/problem "Given that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $5$, which of the following statements are true?

I. $P \cdot Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$,

II. $P + Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $5$,

III. $\dfrac{P}{Q}$ is sometimes a polynomial." :question/worked-solution "Let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. The highest-degree terms in $P$ and $Q$ must both contain $x^5.$ Therefore, the highest-degree term in $P \cdot Q$ must contain $x^5 \cdot x^5 = x^{5+5} = x^{10},$ meaning that $P \cdot Q$ has degree $10.$

- Statement II is false. For example, suppose that $P=x^5$ and $Q=-x^5.$ Then $P+Q = x^5+(-x^5)=0,$ which is not a polynomial of degree $5.$

- Statement III is true. For example, suppose that $P=x^5$ and $Q=x^5.$ Then $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{x^5}{x^5} = 1,$ which is a polynomial of degree $0.$

In conclusion, only statements I and III are true."} {:db/id 17592186092714 :question/id #uuid "5f528577-792d-5dde-937b-39993322cd56" :question/math-academy-id "q-46457"} {:db/id 17592186092726 942} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186093195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093471 :tutorial/content "Consider the following polynomials:

$$
P(x) = 2x^{\color{blue}4} - 3x + 1, \qquad
Q(x) = -6x^{\color{red}3} + 5x^2 + x
$$

Notice that these polynomials have degrees $4$ and $3,$ respectively. We write this as

$$
\textrm{deg}(P) = {\color{blue}4}, \qquad
\textrm{deg}(Q) = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Furthermore, 

- the leading term in $P(x)$ is $2x^{\color{blue}4},$ and

- the leading term in $Q(x)$ is $-6x^{\color{red}3}$

As a result, the leading term in the product $P \cdot Q$ equals the product of the leading terms of $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
2x^{\color{blue}4} \cdot (-6x^{\color{red}3}) = -12x^{{\color{blue}4}+{\color{red}3}} = -12x^{\color{purple}7}
$$

Therefore, the degree of $P \cdot Q$ must be ${\color{purple}{7}}.$

We have the following general rule:

*The degree of the product of two polynomials equals the sum of the degrees of these polynomials:* 

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \cdot Q) = \textrm{deg}(P) + \textrm{deg}(Q)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60187490-7cd6-566d-ab45-128e2c4f81c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6201 :tutorial/title "The Degree of a Product of Two Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f1dac5f5-12ea-56be-8067-1b9f815159f5" :step/math-academy-id 37591 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093196}} {:db/id 17592186093196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092312 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186092159 :question/id #uuid "d0f6fda4-4083-5541-8f0e-9a61f740ba8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9981"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f497212-3946-51e1-9c39-45284ab55da6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048406} {:db/id 17592186049729}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092555} {:db/id 17592186092711} {:db/id 17592186272251} {:db/id 17592186292688} {:db/id 17592186294932} {:db/id 17592186294933} {:db/id 17592186329775} {:db/id 17592186385158} {:db/id 17592186435057} {:db/id 17592186435059}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Degree of a Product of Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "7e843dd4-2f8a-5237-87b2-28b5a09adb3d" :step/math-academy-id 37594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093197}} {:db/id 17592186093197 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093472 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the degree of the sum and difference of two polynomials $P$ and $Q.$ 

First, let's suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have *different* degrees. In this case, the degree of the sum or difference equals the largest of the two degrees. We write

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \pm Q) = \max \big\{ \textrm{deg}(P), \textrm{deg}(Q) \big\},
$$

 
where the $\textrm{max}$ function simply returns the largest element of the set.

For example, suppose that $\textrm{deg}(P) = 5$ and $\textrm{deg}(Q) = 2.$ Then,

$$
\textrm{deg}(P + Q) = \max \big\{ 5, 2 \big\} = 5.
$$

 

To see why this is true, note that the leading term of $P$ contains an $x^5,$ and the leading term of $Q$ has an $x^2.$ When we add the two polynomials, no term of $Q$ could cancel out the leading term of $P.$ So the sum of the polynomials must have degree $5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fae91d47-b786-5c2f-9a29-dfb06624930f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6202 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 1"} :step/id #uuid "82947aff-7f67-51bc-9a88-6e5d204e1c08" :step/math-academy-id 37596 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093199}} {:db/id 17592186093198 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093473 :tutorial/content "Polynomials are also closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but not closed under division.

To illustrate, let's consider the following two polynomials:

$$
P(x) = x+1, \qquad Q(x) = x^2
$$

- When we *add* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P+Q & =(x+1)+({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *subtract* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P-Q & =(x+1)-({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1-{x}^{2} \\  & =-{x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *multiply* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P\cdot Q & =(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}) \\  & =x\cdot {x}^{2}+1\cdot {x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- However, *dividing* the two polynomials does *not* give a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{P}{Q} & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

**Watch Out!** Although polynomials are not closed under division, the ratio of two polynomials is *sometimes* a polynomial. For example, if $P=x^2$ and $Q=x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{P}{Q} =  \dfrac{x^2}{x} = x,
$$

which is a polynomial." :tutorial/id #uuid "d529e51a-742c-52f5-874b-546cf98a1849" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6228 :tutorial/title "Closure Properties of Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "2236e99f-a53e-57c2-91ab-c3091e8a86a9" :step/math-academy-id 37829 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093231}} {:db/id 17592186093199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093474 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have the *same* degree. That is

$$
\textrm{deg}(P) =   \textrm{deg}(Q) = n.
$$

 

In this case, the degree of the sum or difference can be *any integer* from $0$ to $n.$

$$
0 \leq \textrm{deg}(P \pm Q) \leq n
$$

 

Let's consider some examples:

- Let $P$ and $Q$ be polynomials of degree $15.$ Then, the *largest possible degree* of $P+Q$ is $15$ since the resulting polynomial can't contain terms of order higher than $15.$

- On the other hand, the *smallest possible degree* of $P+Q$ is $0.$ For instance, suppose $P=x^{15}$ and $Q=1-x^{15}.$ Then $P +Q = 1,$ which is a polynomial of degree $0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f9d9fe12-e873-5b5b-aca8-f212f9be62b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6229 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 2"} :step/id #uuid "6b4c7081-0037-5d22-8c22-bf18957c01d2" :step/math-academy-id 37830 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093232}} {:db/id 17592186093230 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093380 :tutorial/content "When we add, subtract, or multiply two integers, the answer is always an integer. 

To illustrate, let's consider the following two integers:

$$
a = 3, \qquad b=2
$$

- When we *add* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a + b = 3+2 = 5\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- When we *subtract* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a - b = 3-2 = 1\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- When we *multiply* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a \cdot b = 3\cdot 2 = 6\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- However, dividing the two integers does *not* give an integer:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac32 \quad{\color{red}{\boldsymbol\times}}
$$

We say the integers are **closed** under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but **not closed** under division.

**Watch Out!** Although integers are not closed under division, the ratio of two integers is *sometimes* an integer. For example, if $a=4$ and $b=2,$ then

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} =  \dfrac{4}{2} = 2,
$$

which is an integer." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7d0a253-b58a-5205-b05d-d5d2f1d49f6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1593 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "90c92812-0369-53f2-8139-3a602c9d8ddf" Therefore, the degree of $P \cdot Q$ must be ${\color{purple}{7}}.$

We have the following general rule:

*The degree of the product of two polynomials equals the sum of the degrees of these polynomials:* 

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \cdot Q) = \textrm{deg}(P) + \textrm{deg}(Q)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60187490-7cd6-566d-ab45-128e2c4f81c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6201 :tutorial/title "The Degree of a Product of Two Polynomials"} {:db/id 17592186093196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092312 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186092159 :question/id #uuid "d0f6fda4-4083-5541-8f0e-9a61f740ba8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9981"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f497212-3946-51e1-9c39-45284ab55da6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048406} {:db/id 17592186049729}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092555} {:db/id 17592186092711} {:db/id 17592186272251} {:db/id 17592186292688} {:db/id 17592186294932} {:db/id 17592186294933} {:db/id 17592186329775} {:db/id 17592186385158} {:db/id 17592186435057} {:db/id 17592186435059}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Degree of a Product of Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "7e843dd4-2f8a-5237-87b2-28b5a09adb3d" :step/math-academy-id 37594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093197}} {:db/id 17592186093197 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093472 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the degree of the sum and difference of two polynomials $P$ and $Q.$ 

First, let's suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have *different* degrees. In this case, the degree of the sum or difference equals the largest of the two degrees. We write

$$
\textrm{deg}(P \pm Q) = \max \big\{ \textrm{deg}(P), \textrm{deg}(Q) \big\},
$$

 
where the $\textrm{max}$ function simply returns the largest element of the set.

For example, suppose that $\textrm{deg}(P) = 5$ and $\textrm{deg}(Q) = 2.$ Then,

$$
\textrm{deg}(P + Q) = \max \big\{ 5, 2 \big\} = 5.
$$

 

To see why this is true, note that the leading term of $P$ contains an $x^5,$ and the leading term of $Q$ has an $x^2.$ When we add the two polynomials, no term of $Q$ could cancel out the leading term of $P.$ So the sum of the polynomials must have degree $5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fae91d47-b786-5c2f-9a29-dfb06624930f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6202 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 1"} :step/id #uuid "82947aff-7f67-51bc-9a88-6e5d204e1c08" :step/math-academy-id 37596 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093199}} {:db/id 17592186093472 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the degree of the sum and difference of two polynomials $P$ and $Q.$

$$

$$

For example, suppose that $\textrm{deg}(P) = 5$ and $\textrm{deg}(Q) = 2.$ Then,

$$
\textrm{deg}(P + Q) = \max \big\{ 5, 2 \big\} = 5.
$$

 

To see why this is true, note that the leading term of $P$ contains an $x^5,$ and the leading term of $Q$ has an $x^2.$ When we add the two polynomials, no term of $Q$ could cancel out the leading term of $P.$ So the sum of the polynomials must have degree $5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fae91d47-b786-5c2f-9a29-dfb06624930f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6202 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 1"} {:db/id 17592186093199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093474 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have the *same* degree. That is

$$
\textrm{deg}(P) =   \textrm{deg}(Q) = n.
$$

 

In this case, the degree of the sum or difference can be *any integer* from $0$ to $n.$

$$
0 \leq \textrm{deg}(P \pm Q) \leq n
$$

 

Let's consider some examples:

- Let $P$ and $Q$ be polynomials of degree $15.$ Then, the *largest possible degree* of $P+Q$ is $15$ since the resulting polynomial can't contain terms of order higher than $15.$

- On the other hand, the *smallest possible degree* of $P+Q$ is $0.$ For instance, suppose $P=x^{15}$ and $Q=1-x^{15}.$ Then $P +Q = 1,$ which is a polynomial of degree $0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f9d9fe12-e873-5b5b-aca8-f212f9be62b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6229 :tutorial/title "Degrees of Sums and Differences of Polynomials: Case 2"} :step/id #uuid "6b4c7081-0037-5d22-8c22-bf18957c01d2" :step/math-academy-id 37830 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093232}} {:db/id 17592186093198 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093473 :tutorial/content "Polynomials are also closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but not closed under division.

To illustrate, let's consider the following two polynomials:

$$
P(x) = x+1, \qquad Q(x) = x^2
$$

- When we *add* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P+Q & =(x+1)+({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *subtract* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P-Q & =(x+1)-({x}^{2}) \\  & =x+1-{x}^{2} \\  & =-{x}^{2}+x+1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- When we *multiply* the two polynomials, we get a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}P\cdot Q & =(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}) \\  & =x\cdot {x}^{2}+1\cdot {x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- However, *dividing* the two polynomials does *not* give a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{P}{Q} & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

**Watch Out!** Although polynomials are not closed under division, the ratio of two polynomials is *sometimes* a polynomial. For example, if $P=x^2$ and $Q=x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{P}{Q} =  \dfrac{x^2}{x} = x,
$$

which is a polynomial." :tutorial/id #uuid "d529e51a-742c-52f5-874b-546cf98a1849" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6228 :tutorial/title "Closure Properties of Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "2236e99f-a53e-57c2-91ab-c3091e8a86a9" :step/math-academy-id 37829 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093231}} {:db/id 17592186093473 :tutorial/content "Polynomials are also closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but not closed under division.

To illustrate, let's consider the following two integers:

$$
a = 3, \qquad b=2
$$

- When we *add* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a + b = 3+2 = 5\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- When we *subtract* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a - b = 3-2 = 1\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- When we *multiply* the two integers, we get an integer:

$$
a \cdot b = 3\cdot 2 = 6\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

- However, dividing the two integers does *not* give an integer:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac32 \quad{\color{red}{\boldsymbol\times}}
$$

We say the integers are **closed** under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but **not closed** under division.

**Watch Out!** Although integers are not closed under division, the ratio of two integers is *sometimes* an integer. For example, if $a=4$ and $b=2,$ then

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} =  \dfrac{4}{2} = 2,
$$

which is an integer." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7d0a253-b58a-5205-b05d-d5d2f1d49f6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1593 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186093233 :step/content {:db/id $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-5)^{2}-3(0-1)^{2} & =0+5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-3 & =5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =4 \\ x-5 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =5\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $x=3$ and $x=7.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(3,0,0)$ and $(7,0,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186339086 :question/id #uuid "3ca33d54-3052-5d14-952c-2bb3467296fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-72301"} {:db/id 17592186339087 :question/id #uuid "14b3d36d-0d61-5644-876e-58f0a854730d" :question/math-academy-id "q-72303"} {:db/id 17592186339088 :question/id #uuid "0b363aae-9a1a-5bd8-a7ce-6affaf56df43" :question/math-academy-id "q-72305" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c67b3b1-ca17-50d9-826b-aa84c548da4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-7,0,0)$ and $(1,0,0)$" :db/id 17592186336743} {:answer/id #uuid "767a3d83-a217-545e-829c-803f0a2e5f93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,0)" :db/id 17592186337098} {:answer/id #uuid "7d9dcfbc-5db8-52dc-aa70-3ce3548a031a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-7,0,0)$ and $(-1,0,0)$" :db/id 17592186337168} {:answer/id #uuid "cd3c3792-dfb7-53e4-8d4f-f13a6930b54d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-7,0,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186337832} {:answer/id #uuid "fb10441f-5dc2-53c4-8a56-253eb94e9ba8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,0,0)$ and $(7,0,0)$" :db/id 17592186338235}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336743} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a0d88c8-d602-5247-ade9-89205172c789" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338432}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x+3)^{2}-2(y-3)^{2}=z-2$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+8={x}^{2}-(y+9)^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+8 & ={x}^{2}-(y+9)^{2} \\ z-(-8) & =\frac{(x-0)^{2}}{1}-\frac{(y-(-9))^{2}}{1}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(0,-9,-8).$"} {:db/id 17592186366233 :question/id #uuid "16658c9e-8fa3-5c30-87d5-30c0a6e7db83" :question/math-academy-id "q-72302" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b4441e7-9ebc-5545-9efa-2ee1440fa1b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0,0)$ and $(0,4,0)$" :db/id 17592186366235} {:answer/id #uuid "6bc6b114-2ad4-5286-98ef-bab6af5d1a58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/id 17592186366236} {:answer/id #uuid "2b746e61-be9d-59cb-8bf8-3b68b34626f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,-4,0)$ and $(0,0,0)$" :db/id 17592186366237} {:answer/id #uuid "e590b348-2055-5203-8c91-c618c41626da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,-4,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186366238} {:answer/id #uuid "84bf4e2c-448d-5b40-8003-6a09149d5ddd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,-2,0)$ and $(0,0,0)$" :db/id 17592186366239}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366237} :answer-field/id #uuid "98778e41-d388-55c7-822d-6a1e70584ae6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366234}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x-6)^{2}-8(y+2)^{2}=z+4$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "To find the $y$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $x=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-6)^{2}-8(y+2)^{2} & =0+4 \\ 36-8(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ 32 & =8(y+2)^{2} \\ (y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ y+2 & =\pm 2 \\ y & =-2\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $y=-4$ and $y=0.$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8$ and the plane 
$z=4$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?" :question/worked-solution "To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=4$, we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=4+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=12 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1893} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125377 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125774 :tutorial/content "Consider the quadric surface with the equation

$$
z = x^2 + y^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/14/14e8d23a4bc649257c2f7351e0d2c1d62e39a8cd8eed1467e65853ee121b836e.png)

 

This surface is an example of an **elliptic paraboloid.**

 The **vertex** of this elliptic paraboloid is located at the origin, and its **axis of symmetry** is the $z$-axis. Note that the axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex.

More generally, the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis whose vertex is at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

These surfaces are called *elliptic* *paraboloids* because their traces in the $xy$-plane are *ellipses*, while their traces in the $yz$- and $xz$-planes are *parabolas*. 17592186125461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125805 :tutorial/content "So far, we've encountered elliptic paraboloids whose axes of symmetry are parallel to the $z$-axis. 
Let's now consider the cases when an elliptic paraboloid is oriented along the $x$- or the $y$-axes.

For an elliptic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows.

- When the vertex is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis:

$$
y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}
$$

![](images/da/da37415ddd27764a719fecc5780ee91e6e8ad3f5ce877101b81d1a955c57eb6f.png)

- When the vertex is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis:

$$
x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}
$$

![](images/d1/d1488d9f4767312795a84ce6441f64dd567223d1de4da66adbd6e39de9612a53.png)

Likewise, for a hyperbolic paraboloid, the other two cases are as follows:

- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $y$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $y$-axis. The two corresponding equations are

$$
y = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}.
$$

- When the saddle point is at the origin and the $x$ term is linear, the axis of symmetry is the $x$-axis. The two corresponding equations are

$$
x = \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f53539f-e8db-5205-b9d0-3919805097ae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3851 :tutorial/title "Alternative Orientations of the Axis of Symmetry"} :step/id #uuid "26ce593b-6eaa-5a9c-a0cc-f0cf3649224d" :step/math-academy-id 22415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125638}} {:db/id 17592186125638 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125880 :tutorial/content "The traces of an elliptic paraboloid are either ellipses, parabolas, a single point, or the empty set.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the elliptic paraboloid given by

$$
z=x^2+y^2.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/02/021dd988863021f564a0e85fb3db93030740059f2a50ade6504b3e12a5665372.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =z \\ {x}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/9f/9f6cd0703b5d7b2458cbfd688d91f08a79752fa1ccd3616e5975f5c017aa7b42.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =z \\ {y}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/89/89be283ed121d3e30b1913e4412b8d3556ed611ef2a9a9bfd686d0594409f5c9.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=-k$ for $k > 0$ is the empty set. This is because $z\geq 0$ everywhere on the elliptic paraboloid.

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=k$ for $k > 0$ is an ellipse:

$$
x^2+y^2 = k
$$

![](images/f1/f15e925431b0d2ccfd4afa703cad1bcb37b65a75e96fbeabcf4823703bf184e5.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0ea2e49f-f5aa-57b1-9b67-de6947a0e6e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7839 :tutorial/title "Traces of Elliptic Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "587634e3-d3a5-57e5-bd78-93b3ed921e5b" :step/math-academy-id 45282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125639}} {:db/id 17592186125639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125881 :tutorial/content "The traces of a hyperbolic paraboloid are either hyperbolas, parabolas, or intersecting lines.

For example, let's find the traces with the coordinate planes for the hyperbolic paraboloid given by

$$
z=x^2-y^2.
$$

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ y & =\pm x\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to two intersecting lines in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9b/9b3fbb9d8945c5d9208a59d404e489e4a339082c602c18154010e3e53083b220.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{0}^{2} & =z \\ z & ={x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to the parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/e8/e8e2b6306052e781fd149e4eebb04da79eddb44b5261b05b129f208ad523b70b.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =z \\ z & =-{y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to the parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/70/7010e4c26af60c6c27f66c93b805a2bac1e191c1646b5aac3a77f5dd3dadc64f.png)

 

In this particular case, the **saddle point** is at the origin. It is a minimum point for the trace in the $xz$-plane but a maximum point for the trace in the $yz$-plane.

Finally, note that the trace of our surface with the plane $z=k\neq 0$ is a hyperbola:

$$
x^2-y^2 = k
$$

![](images/b9/b9c1baab2f9d85c2c415cae91908d5c908aa0b1cef1eb8b5901f7f3b78bf66b2.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c2467f92-856a-5690-bd8d-1c593268396a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7840 :tutorial/title "Traces of Hyperbolic Paraboloids"} :step/id #uuid "d9e46e54-59aa-5284-ac11-65d16e6bca74" :step/math-academy-id 45283 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125460}}] :activity/title "Paraboloids" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124696} {:db/id 17592186125377 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125774 :tutorial/content "Consider the quadric surface with the equation

$$
z = x^2 + y^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/14/14e8d23a4bc649257c2f7351e0d2c1d62e39a8cd8eed1467e65853ee121b836e.png)

 

This surface is an example of an **elliptic paraboloid.**

 The **vertex** of this elliptic paraboloid is located at the origin, and its **axis of symmetry** is the $z$-axis. Note that the axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex.

More generally, the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis whose vertex is at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

These surfaces are called *elliptic* *paraboloids* because their traces in the $xy$-plane are *ellipses*, while their traces in the $yz$- and $xz$-planes are *parabolas*. We'll discuss the traces of this surface in more detail shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "d5da7d20-bcec-546d-8cd6-178215fc2096" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3439 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0155d173-f619-5729-9721-6203bf768219" :step/math-academy-id 19459 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125378}} {:db/id 17592186125774 :tutorial/content "Consider the quadric surface with the equation

- The trace of this surface in the $xy$-plane (when $z=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which corresponds to the origin $(0,0,0).$

![](images/02/021dd988863021f564a0e85fb3db93030740059f2a50ade6504b3e12a5665372.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $xz$-plane (when $y=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =z \\ {x}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/9f/9f6cd0703b5d7b2458cbfd688d91f08a79752fa1ccd3616e5975f5c017aa7b42.png)

 

- The trace of this surface in the $yz$-plane (when $x=0$) is given by the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =z \\ {y}^{2} & =z,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a parabola in the $yz$-plane that has its vertex at the origin.

![](images/89/89be283ed121d3e30b1913e4412b8d3556ed611ef2a9a9bfd686d0594409f5c9.png)

There are a few other cases we should note:

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=-k$ for $k > 0$ is the empty set. This is because $z\geq 0$ everywhere on the elliptic paraboloid.

- The trace of our surface with the plane $z=k$ for $k > 0$ is an ellipse:

$$
x^2+y^2 = k
$$

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is negative semi-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are non-positive.

- Quadratic form II is *not* negative semi-definite since all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive.

- Quadratic form III is *not* negative semi-definite since some of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ is positive).

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form II is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive (${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form III is positive-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive.

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=9$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -45 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-5,\,9.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186162010 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161802 :question/id #uuid "fa658f82-1d0b-54a3-a172-4d59f03f629e" 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=9$ and $det(A)=18$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=9$ and 

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}|=18.
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=9>0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}|=18>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186162639 :question/id #uuid "1a18cc33-e8b9-51a0-9ec6-b247bdd1e062" :question/math-academy-id "q-94467"} {:db/id 17592186269225 Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-5$ and $det(A)>0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-5$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot 1 \\  & =-8<0.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-8<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

:topic/math-academy-id 3127} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162855 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163230 :tutorial/content "In certain applications involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

We classify quadratic forms using the following terminology:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](images/09/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](images/f4/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6542a88-fba4-557b-ae08-48d95747b079" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4889 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6be8e550-b338-5637-a624-ef1b87eabd9b" :step/math-academy-id 30543 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162895}} {:db/id 17592186162895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161800 :question/id #uuid "f3f6f5b1-bc25-586c-9d4d-dfeb64cfa077" :question/math-academy-id "e-8262"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6289ad34-2393-5f5f-b7f0-a1ab1a3916f4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049450}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162634} {:db/id 17592186162635} {:db/id 17592186269218} {:db/id 17592186360479} {:db/id 17592186360480} {:db/id 17592186360482} {:db/id 17592186491992} {:db/id 17592186492023} {:db/id 17592186492064}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Possible Quadratic Form Types Using Substitution"} :step/id #uuid "ca8c0245-0936-52e2-ab35-4e10d9592791" :step/math-academy-id 30875 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163054}} {:db/id 17592186162896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163241 :tutorial/content "Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Using the same criteria, we can also classify the symmetric matrix $A$ as positive-definite, positive semi-definite, etc.

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/85/8582c8b840b1e4696b9f83cb2c117d67e3b832e40b1ded716e0dcd23752c6f9c.svg)

Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +6) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-4,\,-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) =  \mathbf{x}^T A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite." :tutorial/id #uuid "c4b47113-5633-5c1b-bb17-e6ec70b5a550" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4952 :tutorial/title "Using Eigenvalues to Classify Quadratic Forms"} :step/id #uuid "2d8db3b7-e619-5958-9482-0acdf61cd3e6" :step/math-academy-id 30876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162897}} {:db/id 17592186162897 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162009 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161801 :question/id #uuid "178e4bbc-718c-5b9e-843a-91914ef16f64" :question/math-academy-id "e-8263"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4105f1cb-eb48-5946-92f7-cd5e67689912" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162636} {:db/id 17592186162637} {:db/id 17592186269221} {:db/id 17592186269222} {:db/id 17592186269223} {:db/id 17592186269224} {:db/id 17592186360498} {:db/id 17592186360499} {:db/id 17592186491989} {:db/id 17592186491990} {:db/id 17592186492017} {:db/id 17592186504680}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Quadratic Form Type by Calculating the Corresponding Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "20343d54-d701-5e59-9cab-48adc9d25870" :step/math-academy-id 30877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163055}} {:db/id 17592186162898 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163242 :tutorial/content "Let ![](images/c6/c6f4a56eed9073b3541e4398db9fc99f2e8ca94f651762e1f650bfe54865ca49.svg) for ![](images/16/1621ad9f5426c8fe19e2d5a00c5f92a60420aeaed7bfe623db70c9ab4e57527d.svg)  denote the leading principal minors of an ![](images/b0/b0cdde792f80dc6b0c5defb2f8d767ae115ecf922fa46f2a233f10959e509870.svg) matrix ![](images/c8/c8c72090d28b539bed2177052b06540383d63ac720008f1b301dafcac4fa6227.svg)

For example, the form $A(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2$ over $\mathbb{R}^2$ is positive semi-definite. Notice that this particular form is not positive-definite since it gives zero on the nonzero vector ![](images/d3/d32277694c7bd75cf76ea413fba14b25a679f84e8194c07af201e103d23a1056.svg)

It's also worth noting that

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](images/09/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](images/f4/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6542a88-fba4-557b-ae08-48d95747b079" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4889 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6be8e550-b338-5637-a624-ef1b87eabd9b" :step/math-academy-id 30543 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162895}} {:db/id 17592186163230 :tutorial/content "In certain applications involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](images/09/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](images/f4/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6542a88-fba4-557b-ae08-48d95747b079" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4889 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186162895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161800 :question/id #uuid "f3f6f5b1-bc25-586c-9d4d-dfeb64cfa077" :question/math-academy-id "e-8262"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6289ad34-2393-5f5f-b7f0-a1ab1a3916f4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049450}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162634} {:db/id 17592186162635} {:db/id 17592186269218} {:db/id 17592186360479} {:db/id 17592186360480} {:db/id 17592186360482} {:db/id 17592186491992} {:db/id 17592186492023} {:db/id 17592186492064}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Possible Quadratic Form Types Using Substitution"} :step/id #uuid "ca8c0245-0936-52e2-ab35-4e10d9592791" :step/math-academy-id 30875 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163054}} {:db/id 17592186163054 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163318 :tutorial/content "There are two further classifications of quadratic forms that turn out to be useful:

- any negative-definite quadratic form is negative semi-definite." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f10e579-6a9a-5929-95df-033a67f11e7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6137 :tutorial/title "Positive and Negative Semi-Definite Quadratic Forms"} :step/id #uuid "2b84589b-e820-5864-af80-1c00cdcc8be5" :step/math-academy-id 37271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162896}} {:db/id 17592186162896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163241 :tutorial/content "Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Using the same criteria, we can also classify the symmetric matrix $A$ as positive-definite, positive semi-definite, etc.

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/85/8582c8b840b1e4696b9f83cb2c117d67e3b832e40b1ded716e0dcd23752c6f9c.svg)

Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +6) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-4,\,-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) =  \mathbf{x}^T A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite." :tutorial/id #uuid "c4b47113-5633-5c1b-bb17-e6ec70b5a550" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4952 :tutorial/title "Using Eigenvalues to Classify Quadratic Forms"} :step/id #uuid "2d8db3b7-e619-5958-9482-0acdf61cd3e6" :step/math-academy-id 30876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162897}} {:db/id 17592186163241 :tutorial/content "Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=9$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -45 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-5,\,9.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "10c29fe9-08fc-5279-949b-8249dea25825" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504719}} {:db/id 17592186504717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360498 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "abae4a38-c5fd-5f02-a772-5aa129094bed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186469734} {:answer/id #uuid "61d28482-9aa5-5496-9fe2-e88afd3b2c83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186469735}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186469734} :answer-field/id #uuid "1888ce5d-ffbd-5ed4-8be1-6bd4f78e3048" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470479} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c36a82ef-f663-5517-a82d-dfb31295d4df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186469736} {:answer/id #uuid "1abaa9d3-1384-5eab-9d1f-4167841b8420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186469737}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186469736} :answer-field/id #uuid "78bab090-2cec-52a7-8c1a-ea25848b4605" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470480} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8053ba89-f2f1-5607-8419-7cfe23f95b4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186469738} {:answer/id #uuid "2a6d6721-833a-5366-b67a-9b57255478fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186469739}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186469739} :answer-field/id #uuid "24fa5bdc-7dac-5793-b27a-1eadf77bbfa1" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470481}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1a997acb-de91-5ebd-a6cc-103226757603" :question/math-academy-id "q-94787" :question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are positive-definite?

A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-5$ and $det(A)>0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-5$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot 1 \\  & =-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements II and III are true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-8<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "3edbcb74-ef0e-5d2b-b4a5-9224616cec9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504735}} {:db/id 17592186504735 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360503 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4e082f9d-d667-53bf-8ebe-ea0165b6dc26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186452107} {:answer/id #uuid "1b961c92-afa7-5358-90fd-24c675c9bd2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186452108}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186452107} :answer-field/id #uuid "b3d091f6-4c30-55e8-95e8-5336bea05763" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452901} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e233fee2-70e2-5e90-896f-04fbc826023e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186452109} {:answer/id #uuid "a851a8d9-1e67-5532-b8dd-92c9d9b65acc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186452110}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186452110} :answer-field/id #uuid "3be5e419-a12d-5643-8194-2d9a2b4897ec" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452902} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f0fe63a9-b90e-5777-b826-3d8827fd649a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186452111} {:answer/id #uuid "1aded71f-8051-53a7-97fa-e199f9608ed3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186452112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186452111} :answer-field/id #uuid "42458164-cc6a-5528-9e47-6288386413d8" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452903}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7d5f731a-8eca-5400-88d7-dd10fc541120" :question/math-academy-id "q-94805" :question/problem "$$

- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form II is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive (${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form III is positive-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive.

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -45 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-5,\,9.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

"43115d1d-8694-5a95-b413-4600fbd2bc68" :question/math-academy-id "q-94804" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-5$ and $det(A)>0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-5$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot 1 \\  & =-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements II and III are true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-8<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "3edbcb74-ef0e-5d2b-b4a5-9224616cec9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504735}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7d5f731a-8eca-5400-88d7-dd10fc541120" :question/math-academy-id "q-94805" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=8$ and $det(A)<0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=8$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}8 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 7 \\  & =21>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=8>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|=7>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=21>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "c73b7c66-857e-5a2c-9637-ba3dda90e9f0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504718}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$
y={e}^{u},\,u=-3x+5.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-3{e}^{u} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3x+5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x+{e}^{-3x+5}) \\  & =8-3{e}^{-3x+5} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3x+5}+8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186314964 :question/id #uuid "8caad42a-7778-5faa-ba43-6f75823507a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-340497"} {:db/id 17592186329850 :question/id #uuid "Given that $y=e^{-x^2},$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = e^u, \qquad u=-x^2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = e^u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-2x{e}^{u} \\  & =-2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092618 :question/id #uuid "0e52fa16-cf3e-5339-95e2-786fe7ef7e5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-1953"} {:db/id 17592186092734 :question/id #uuid $$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-6{x}^{2}) \\  & =-6{x}^{2}{e}^{8-2{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}

differentiate exponential functions like 

$$
y = e^{3x}.
$$

First, notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = e^u, \qquad u = 3x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({e}^{u})\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x) \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 3 \\  & =3{e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=3x,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cf67b8fb-2658-5221-b309-6cf09e93b5e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1268 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "87b44f73-3af6-53c8-a8c8-61525491b5d4" :step/math-academy-id
