\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)} & ={\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)}|}_{x=7} \\  & =\frac{f(7)}{{7}^{2}\cdot g(7)} \\  & =\frac{0}{49\cdot 0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{(f(x))^{′}}{({x}^{2}g(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 7}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2xg(x)+{x}^{2}{g}^{′}(x)}|}_{x=7} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(7)}{2\cdot 7\cdot g(7)+{7}^{2}\cdot {g}^{′}(7)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+49\cdot 2} \\  & =\frac{1}{98}\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=2$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3} & ={\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3}|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2+g(2)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(2)+2-3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2+3}-\sqrt{5}}{1+2-3} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5})^{′}}{(f(x)+x-3)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=2$ again, and this time, we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1} & ={\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(x)}{2\sqrt{x+g(x)}}}{{f}^{′}(x)+1}|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1+{g}^{′}(2)}{2\sqrt{2+g(2)}}}{{f}^{′}(2)+1} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1+4}{2\sqrt{5}}}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{5}{8\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+g(x)}-\sqrt{5}}{f(x)+x-3}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{8}.

and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $10$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $3$ | $-20$ | $-2$ | $-6$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=10$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)} & ={\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{f(10)+5}{20+g(10)} \\  & =\frac{-5+5}{20+(-20)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{(f(x)+5)^{′}}{(2x+g(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=10$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(10)}{2+{g}^{′}(10)} \\  & =\frac{0}{2+(-2)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)}{2+{g}^{′}(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{({f}^{′}(x))^{′}}{(2+{g}^{′}(x))^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=10,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)}|}_{x=10} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{″}(10)}{{g}^{″}(10)} \\  & =\frac{3}{-6} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 10}\frac{f(x)+5}{2x+g(x)}=-\frac{1}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186101226 :question/id #uuid "880c0535-3390-5162-8b8d-aefb96cc0d7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-16175"} {:db/id 17592186234323 :question/id #uuid "fed62691-6668-5c74-90ca-07c937644bed" :question/math-academy-id "q-72361"} {:db/id 17592186508039 :question/id #uuid "04a061b7-e5c9-583d-9ee4-5ed73b8719bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-337014" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cdf52d1c-d0cf-596a-b9d3-a36801c3cff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186507883}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507883} :answer-field/id #uuid "4aaa0726-be5f-51d0-b8c1-e8e9cc273212" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186507972}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $e$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Using the values from the table, evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-x\,f(x)}{\,f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}\,}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{1}-1\cdot f(1)}{f(1)g(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-e}{(e)(1)-e} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-xf(x))^{′}}{(f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, and once more we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{e}^{1}-(f(1)+1\cdot {f}^{′}(1))}{{f}^{′}(1)g(1)+f(1){g}^{′}(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-(e+0)}{(0)(1)+(e)(1)-e} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x)))^{′}}{({f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(2{f}^{′}(x)+x{f}^{″}(x))}{{f}^{″}(x)g(x)+2{f}^{′}(x){g}^{′}(x)+f(x){g}^{″}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute $x=1$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{e}^{x}-(2{f}^{′}(x)+x{f}^{″}(x))}{{f}^{″}(x)g(x)+2{f}^{′}(x){g}^{′}(x)+f(x){g}^{″}(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{e}^{1}-(2{f}^{′}(1)+1\cdot {f}^{″}(1))}{{f}^{″}(1)g(1)+2{f}^{′}(1){g}^{′}(1)+f(1){g}^{″}(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-(2(0)+0)}{(0)(1)+2(0)(1)+(e)(2)-e} \\  & =\frac{e}{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-x\,f(x)}{\,f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}\,}=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186508078 :question/id #uuid "8771f8a8-d420-525c-a30c-b75746b0e1ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-337304" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52ad2c6b-d809-5214-a3b9-4020cbd24ed3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186507723}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507723} :answer-field/id #uuid "02cd3c44-7134-56fe-b1d4-7d91f48f8a31" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186507945}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $1$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $4$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $2$ |

Using the values from the table, evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\,f(x)+{x}^{2}-3\,}{\,g(x)+{x}^{2}-4\,}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4} & ={\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+{1}^{2}-3}{g(1)+{1}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{2+1-3}{3+1-4} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+{x}^{2}-3)^{′}}{(g(x)+{x}^{2}-4)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, and once more we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)+2(1)}{{g}^{′}(1)+2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-2+2}{-2+2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}}{({g}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we substitute $x=1$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{″}(1)+2}{{g}^{″}(1)+2} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\,f(x)+{x}^{2}-3\,}{\,g(x)+{x}^{2}-4\,}=\frac{3}{2}.

determine the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we first cancel any common factors in the numerator and denominator. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x$.

For example, let's try to find the vertical asymptotes of the rational function $y=\dfrac{2}{x-5}.$ 

Now, there are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, and so we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =x-5 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is a vertical asymptote at $x=5.$

cancel any common factors in the numerator and denominator. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x$.

For example, let's try to find the vertical asymptotes of the rational function $y=\dfrac{2}{x-5}.$ 

Now, there are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, and so we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =x-5 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is a vertical asymptote at $x=5.$

This matches up  with what we see in the graph of the function:

[{:db/id 17592186064988 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065346 :tutorial/content "The **mean value theorem** states that for any function that is continuous and differentiable on some interval, there is some point where the derivative of the function is equal to the slope between the endpoints. More precisely, that is:

> *If $f(x)$ is a function that's continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then there exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> f'(c) = \dfrac {f(b) - f(a)} {b-a}.
> $$

Let's illustrate this idea with an example. Consider the graph of the function 

$$
y = f(x) = 6 - \dfrac 4 x
$$

that's defined on the closed interval $[1,4].$

![](images/fd/fd4d75f2ed0db427c2e3bd41335ceb302c3126781f595c8c21ec914e50f82f64.png)

The line $l_1$ is the secant line that intersects the curve at the endpoints of the interval. The mean value theorem guarantees that there is some special point inside the interval where the tangent line has the same slope as $l_1.$ 

In the diagram above, the special point is $(2,4),$ and the tangent line $l_2$ at this point is parallel to the secant line $l_1.$

To double-check that $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel, we can compute their slopes. The line $l_1$ passes through the points $(1,f(1))$ and $(4,f(4)),$ so its slope is given by 

$$
m=\dfrac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1} =  \dfrac{5-2}{4-1} = 1.
$$

On the other hand, the slope of the line $l_2$ can be found by calculating $f'(2).$

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac{4}{x^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(2) = 1
$$

Since the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ have the same slope, they are parallel." :tutorial/id #uuid "baf78b35-04c6-5d1c-913f-e0a3da70cd8f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2659 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120973 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121072 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a function $f(x) = x^2+2x,$ and we want to find the derivative of the *inverse* function $(f^{-1})'(x).$ Can we do this without explicitly computing the inverse?

Indeed, we can! The trick is to write the inverse function *implicitly*, differentiate it, and then write the result in terms of $f^{-1}(x).$

**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y = x^2+2x,$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$
x=y^2+2y
$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y=f^{-1}(x).$ Also, remember that swapping $x$ and $y$ gives us the inverse function because the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ can be obtained by reflecting the graph of $f(x)$ over the line $y=x.$

![](images/56/56c3c733ec9ed00563b5f5c786175898ac6e564658d1a70d4105f749664436ab.png)

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we start by computing $\dfrac{ \textrm dx}{\textrm dy}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}+2y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}+2y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =2y+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we take the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}y}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}y} = 2y + 2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2y+2}
$$

**Step 3:** Lastly, we write the result in terms of $f^{-1}(x).$ Since $y=f^{-1}(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2y+2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{f}^{-1}(x)] & =\frac{1}{2{f}^{-1}(x)+2} \\ ({f}^{-1})^{'}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{f}^{-1}(x)+2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "28adec60-b1b0-5bee-949f-2d6ac5eefe88" :tutorial/math-academy-id 443 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0eafffd9-cdc6-547a-8dec-831c2199ceb7" :step/math-academy-id :tutorial/content "Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ≈\frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cc2d207-71d4-53a4-8c67-5af0c5f4d173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 371 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a635f38c-a7e9-57d1-aeb5-e9fe6f8751e0" :step/math-academy-id 694}] :activity/title "Estimating Derivatives Using a Backward Difference Quotient" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092467} {:db/id 17592186093335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093444 :tutorial/content "To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ≈\frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cc2d207-71d4-53a4-8c67-5af0c5f4d173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 371 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a635f38c-a7e9-57d1-aeb5-e9fe6f8751e0" :step/math-academy-id 694} {:db/id 17592186093444 :tutorial/content "To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}
$$

for small values of the step size $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is known as the **backward difference approximation** because if $h>0$ then $x-h$ is a step behind $x$ (i.e., to the left). 

![](images/dd/ddc03ba86c8c343d5733b51444cec157182894b6d0c4fccb501b1dc3bca98f57.png)

As usual, the smaller the step size $h$ is, the better the approximation to $f'(x)$ we obtain." :tutorial/id #uuid "6aff8fa6-f787-5984-944a-5648207e6830" :tutorial/math-academy-id 368 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186093336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092390 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186091959 :question/id #uuid "7a6fbfc8-cd6d-57fe-bcab-ab68339683bd" :question/math-academy-id "e-155"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "494ef4f7-873c-5d87-85e5-89094c6cc376" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049061} {:db/id 17592186049362}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092920} {:db/id 17592186092921} {:db/id 17592186317435} {:db/id 17592186317436} {:db/id 17592186317437} {:db/id 17592186339050} {:db/id 17592186339053} {:db/id 17592186508041} {:db/id 17592186508094} {:db/id 17592186508101}] :knowledge-point/title "Estimating a Derivative Given a Table Using a Backward Difference Approximation"} :step/id #uuid "f1579afd-f8b8-522d-815c-72dc7b18e4b7" :step/math-academy-id 687 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093089}} {:db/id 17592186093445 :tutorial/content "Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? $$
x= y^3+y
$$

We say that the equation of this curve is defined **implicitly** because instead of the usual [math]y = y(x),[/math] we have [math]x = x(y).[/math] Sometimes, it's convenient to define a curve this way. You'll meet more implicit curves later.

To graph this curve, we can start by selecting some values of [math]y[/math] and computing the corresponding [math]x[/math]-values as follows:

\begin{align}
	y=0 & \quad \longrightarrow\quad  x=0^3+0=0 \\[5pt]
	y=1 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x=1^3+1=2  \\[5pt]
	y=2 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x=2^3+2=10 \\[5pt]
\end{align}

So we get the points [math](0,0),[/math] [math](2,1),[/math] and [math](10,2).[/math] If we plot these points and connect them with a smooth curve, we get the following graph:

Plotting this curve in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/81/812db123dd422ff781472c73156a2f4d6e88a99aa3726668cd7a8b8882d6e0a8.png)

To find the slope of the tangent to this curve at a point, we need to follow two steps.

- First, we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}$ by differentiating the equation of the curve with respect to $y.$

- Then, we find $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}$ by taking the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac1{\left(\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}\right)}
$$

We'll explore some intuition behind this result at the end of the lesson, but for now, let's focus on carrying out the computation.

We start by differentiating $x=y^3+y$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}+y) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y) \\  & =3{y}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take its reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative is also defined implicitly. In other words, $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}$ is a function of $y,$ not $x.$

To calculate the slope of the tangent to this curve at a point, say $(2,{\color{blue}{1}}),$ we substitute ${\color{blue}{y}} = {\color{blue}{1}}$ into our expression for $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(2,1)} & =\frac{1}{3(1)^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)$ equals $\dfrac14.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5b0053f2-47f3-5689-bf17-ed5cb69d36ff" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7757 :tutorial/title \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}
$$

 

represents the change in $x$ *per unit change* in $y$ at $P.$ According to our diagram, this is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{run}}{\text{rise}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the slope of the tangent to the curve at $P$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{run}}{\text{rise}})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}.\end{aligned}
$$

This result can also be proved formally using the so-called **chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "2683a80b-0267-5fa3-b804-8d7b2373d85b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7758 :tutorial/title "Justification of the Formula"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186106842} :activity/id #uuid "c471a240-0edb-515b-884e-6ed88399df87" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050400 :topic/id #uuid "45b70174-b66e-5c6c-b00b-00ab595d2c86" :topic/math-academy-id 1282} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107143 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute derivatives of composite functions when given function data at specific points.

The values of $f$ and $f'$ are given in the following table:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $2$ | $0$ | $4$ |

Let's find

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to 2} \dfrac{f(x)}{x^3-8}
$$

Notice that if we try to substitute $x=2$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form

$$
\dfrac{0}{0}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(f(x))/(x^{3} - 8) &= \left.(f(x))/(x^{3} - 8)\right|_{x = 2} \\
&= (f(2))/(2^{3} - 8) \\
&= \frac{0}{8 - 8} \\
&= \frac{0}{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(f(x))/(x^{3} - 8) &= lim_(x → 2)((f(x))^{′})/((x^{3} - 8)^{′}) \\
&= lim_(x → 2)(f^{′}(x))/(3x^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=2$ again, and this time, we are able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(f^{′}(x))/(3x^{2}) &= \left.(f^{′}(x))/(3x^{2})\right|_{x = 2} \\
&= (f^{′}(2))/(3 \cdot 2^{2}) \\
&= \frac{4}{3 \cdot 2^{2} - 0} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to 2} \dfrac{f(x)}{x^3-8}=\dfrac{1}{3}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c8d2f073-f126-5950-9555-61f8a6dd159a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 599 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e4ea661d-9e67-59ef-ae74-3ef55f82ab3a" :step/math-academy-id 1137 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101584}} {:db/id 17592186101584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100811 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100623 :question/id #uuid "127247a2-3209-51aa-acb1-eceeaa0dec33" :question/math-academy-id "e-304"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c185115e-e3ce-5503-ab5f-a3d0b1a49cfd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050961} {:db/id 17592186051036}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101223} {:db/id 17592186101224} {:db/id 17592186508115}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Limit of a Function Given as a Table of Values Using L'Hopital's Rule"} :step/id #uuid "06be6b30-b825-5dbe-9087-f089e5a3c396" :step/math-academy-id 1138 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101585}} {:db/id 17592186101585 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100812 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100624 :question/id #uuid "89a99552-00c5-5850-a567-1b338ab5e16b" :question/math-academy-id "e-305"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "98e43a1e-2073-593b-9b55-4f9c25c356a8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101225} {:db/id 17592186101226} {:db/id 17592186234323} {:db/id 17592186508039} {:db/id 17592186508078}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Limit of a Function Given as a Table of Values Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice"} :step/id #uuid "97a0a8f1-3fcd-5681-9176-f997a3d0c81b" :step/math-academy-id 1142}] :activity/title "L'Hopital's Rule Applied to Tables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186101065} {:db/id 17592186101583 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101997 :tutorial/content "The function $f(x)$ is differentiable on an open interval containing $x=2$. So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+{x}^{2}-3}{g(x)+{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+{x}^{2}-3)^{′}}{(g(x)+{x}^{2}-4)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)+2(1)}{{g}^{′}(1)+2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-2+2}{-2+2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+2x}{{g}^{′}(x)+2x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}}{({g}^{′}(x)+2x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{f}^{″}(x)+2}{{g}^{″}(x)+2}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{f}^{″}(1)+2}{{g}^{″}(1)+2} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-xf(x)}{f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-xf(x))^{′}}{(f(x)g(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}}|}_{x=1} & =\frac{{e}^{1}-(f(1)+1\cdot {f}^{′}(1))}{{f}^{′}(1)g(1)+f(1){g}^{′}(1)-{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{e-(e+0)}{(0)(1)+(e)(1)-e} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x))}{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({e}^{x}-(f(x)+x{f}^{′}(x)))^{′}}{({f}^{′}(x)g(x)+f(x){g}^{′}(x)-{e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{e}^{x}-(2{f}^{′}(x)+x{f}^{″}(x))}{{f}^{″}(x)g(x)+2{f}^{′}(x){g}^{′}(x)+f(x){g}^{″}(x)-{e}^{x}}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

:step/next {:db/id 17592186189221}} {:db/id 17592186189114 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189379 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if, for all $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ and $B\subseteq \mathbb R,$ we have

$$
P(X\in A, Y\in B)=P(X\in A)\cdot P(Y\in B).
$$

In practice, this is not a very helpful definition when checking for independence since it involves verifying that it's true for all possible subsets $A$ and $B!$

Now suppose that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ and $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$ are the marginal density functions of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. Then, it can be shown that $X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all values of $x$ and $y.$ Notice that this has a direct analogy with the case of independence for discrete random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "c151ba98-beac-55c8-9a33-b3f619f0a290" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "074fbae0-d9f5-5e1f-8944-2352a5ff16a7" :step/math-academy-id 38083 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189079}} {:db/id 17592186189221 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189419 :tutorial/content "For continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ whose joint support $S$ is rectangular, we have the following theorem:

*Suppose that the joint support of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is rectangular. If 

$$
f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y)
$$

for some two functions $g$ and $h$ (not necessarily probability density functions), then $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Note that the rectangular joint support $S$ does not need to be finite.* 

For example, let's consider the random variables $X$ and $Y$ with the following joint PDF:

![](images/01/01a68d0e42bc71729543e74722390291787ce60530c2432ffa0cdf6c0bb5f093.svg)

The joint support $[0,2]\times [0, \infty)$ is rectangular. Also, we can write $f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y),$ where

$$
g(x) = \dfrac14 x, \qquad h(y) = e^{-y/2}.
$$

Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "9e6987fa-0133-5b85-b6a5-e58a401020b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6534 :tutorial/title "Independence When the Joint Support Is Rectangular"} :step/id #uuid "260c1a0b-a4ec-5618-9cb3-1bfc17d53a21" :step/math-academy-id 39479}] :activity/title "Independence of Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188458} {:db/id 17592186189114 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189379 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "9e6987fa-0133-5b85-b6a5-e58a401020b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6534 :tutorial/title "Independence When the Joint Support Is Rectangular"} :step/id #uuid "260c1a0b-a4ec-5618-9cb3-1bfc17d53a21" :step/math-academy-id 39479} {:db/id 17592186189379 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if, for all $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ and $B\subseteq \mathbb R,$ we have

$$
P(X\in A, Y\in B)=P(X\in A)\cdot P(Y\in B).
$$

In practice, this is not a very helpful definition when checking for independence since it involves verifying that it's true for all possible subsets $A$ and $B!$

Now suppose that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ and $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$ are the marginal density functions of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. Then, it can be shown that $X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all values of $x$ and $y.$ Notice that this has a direct analogy with the case of independence for discrete random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "c151ba98-beac-55c8-9a33-b3f619f0a290" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186189419 :tutorial/content "For continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ whose joint support $S$ is rectangular, we have the following theorem:

*Suppose that the joint support of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is rectangular. If 

$$
f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y)
$$

for some two functions $g$ and $h$ (not necessarily probability density functions), then $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Note that the rectangular joint support $S$ does not need to be finite.* 

For example, let's consider the random variables $X$ and $Y$ with the following joint PDF:

![](images/01/01a68d0e42bc71729543e74722390291787ce60530c2432ffa0cdf6c0bb5f093.svg)

The joint support $[0,2]\times [0, \infty)$ is rectangular. Also, we can write $f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y),$ where

$$
g(x) = \dfrac14 x, \qquad h(y) = e^{-y/2}.
$$

Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "9e6987fa-0133-5b85-b6a5-e58a401020b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6534 :tutorial/title "Independence When the Joint Support Is Rectangular"} [{:db/id 17592186116148 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116503 :tutorial/content "In general, for $k>0$,

- the graph of $y=f(x-k)$ is a horizontal translation of $y=f(x)$ by $k$ units to the *right*, while
- the graph of $y=f(x+k)$ is a horizontal translation of $y=f(x)$ by $k$ units to the *left*.

**Watch out!** It may seem counterintuitive that subtracting $k$ moves the graph to the right, while adding $k$ moves the graph to the left. However, this is in fact true.

To see why, let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below. Let's use this graph to plot the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

![](images/6c/6ca96bba855899f9b87ae06c166503c9af739fcd6bb2ec466a73b75cc70dde7f.png)

Let's take some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ and find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(x-2)$.

For example, take the point $(3,-4)$. The fact that it's on the graph of $y=f(x)$ means that

$$
f(3)=-4
$$

Then if

$$
x={\color{red}5}
$$

we have

$$
f(x-2) = f({\color{red}5}-2) = f(3) = -4
$$

which means that $({\color{red}5},-4)$ is on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ with the same $y$-value and a $x$-value that is $2$ units *greater*! Several more examples of points are shown below.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math] & Points on [math]y=f(x-2)[/math] \\ (3,-4) & (5,-4) \\ (1, 2) & (3, 2) \\ (0, 1.5) & (2, 1.5) \\ (-2, 0) & (0, 0)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's plot both curves.

![](images/ed/edae088984432dc7d0fff816a9e016ad221a3c897a78cf79efe6c784fa9176fe.png)

We see that every point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ is shifted $2$ units *to the right* of the corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "da231b95-be14-58c3-a8fe-6261d61c7d83" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3280 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6345469f-1236-5eaf-8f5f-c51d47bf4f3c" :step/math-academy-id 18017 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116149}} {:db/id 17592186116149 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115259 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115088 :question/id #uuid "e320a97a-d524-5225-895e-76034e599fa9" :question/math-academy-id "e-4973"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "372e7248-7fe0-5138-896d-61b4866f83cd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050647}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115506} {:db/id 17592186115507}] :knowledge-point/title "Plotting a Horizontal Translation of a Given Graph"} :step/id #uuid "d171b522-79a1-5dbc-bcf1-aa7179ecd080" :step/math-academy-id 18018 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116150}} {:db/id 17592186116150 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115260 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115089 :question/id #uuid "4dec57af-1c02-56fe-b38e-e62795fdc93d" :question/math-academy-id "e-4974"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "919da198-25e0-5b6f-8d99-79f1508759b9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115620} {:db/id 17592186115622}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Corresponding Point on a Horizontally Translated Function"} :step/id #uuid "b5c16920-e146-5ef0-841d-e2645a4e1de6" :step/math-academy-id 18019 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116151}} {:db/id 17592186116151 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116504 :tutorial/content "When graphing a function, we can combine vertical and horizontal translations. We start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a}

Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.

$$

\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{sine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \sin(\omega_n x).

- the free terms, and

- a $2\times 2$ linear system for $(a_n,b_n)$ for each $n\ge 1$.

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).

17592186124658 17592186045417] [17592186125892 1064 "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** 

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution:

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{\frac{1}{8},\begin{vmatrix}6 \le x \le 14 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \ge 9) &= \int_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}dx \\
&= \frac{1}{8}\int_{9}^{14}dx \\
&= \frac{1}{8}[x]_{9}^{14} \\
&= \frac{1}{8}[14 - 9] \\
&= \frac{5}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= \frac{a + b}{2} \\
&= \frac{6 + 14}{2} \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

We classify quadratic forms using the following terminology:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](images/09/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](images/f4/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186163230 1065 4889 17592186045417] [17592186163230 1066 #uuid "c6542a88-fba4-557b-ae08-48d95747b079" 17592186045417] [17592186163230 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186163241 1064 "Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^(^) &= 2.5x + 165 \\
&= 2.5(82) + 165 \\

\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - y^(^) \\
&= 360 - 370 \\
&=-10
\end{aligned}

17592186045417] [17592186107178 1064 "The shape below consists of $6$ line segments defined by the $6$ points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and $F.$ These line segments form a loop. 

![](images/25/259bfd166a7870bd1a057b28d4b3324f3b98d05222596f1426afa01d6573e3d8.png)

A chain of straight line segments that form a loop is called a **polygon**.

The line segments are the **sides** of the polygon, and the endpoints of the sides are the **vertices**.

For this polygon:

- The $6$ vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and $F.$

- The $6$ sides are $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$, $\overline{CD}$, $\overline{DE}$, $\overline{EF}$, and $\overline{AF}.$

To denote a particular polygon, we start at one vertex and loop around the polygon, reading off the vertices in order. So, the polygon above can be denoted $ABCDEF.$

The singular form of the word *vertices* is **vertex**. - Two *sides* are **adjacent** (or **consecutive**) if they have a common vertex.

- Two *vertices* are **adjacent** if there is a side joining them.

![](images/6d/6d857920609da14fb0b31f762400c5f54e9e428717c2b55fcb17215280bbbfed.png)

- A **diagonal** is a line segment that joins two non-adjacent vertices.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =40%\times 200 \\  & =0.4\times 200 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac{4}{x^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(2) = 1
$$

**Watch out!** It may seem counterintuitive that subtracting $k$ moves the graph to the right, while adding $k$ moves the graph to the left. However, this is in fact true.

To see why, let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below. Let's use this graph to plot the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

![](images/6c/6ca96bba855899f9b87ae06c166503c9af739fcd6bb2ec466a73b75cc70dde7f.png)

Let's take some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ and find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(x-2)$.

For example, take the point $(3,-4)$. The fact that it's on the graph of $y=f(x)$ means that

$$
f(3)=-4
$$

Then if

$$
x={\color{red}5}
$$

we have

$$
f(x-2) = f({\color{red}5}-2) = f(3) = -4
$$

which means that $({\color{red}5},-4)$ is on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$.

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ with the same $y$-value and a $x$-value that is $2$ units *greater*! Several more examples of points are shown below.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math] & Points on [math]y=f(x-2)[/math] \\ (3,-4) & (5,-4) \\ (1, 2) & (3, 2) \\ (0, 1.5) & (2, 1.5) \\ (-2, 0) & (0, 0)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's plot both curves.

![](images/ed/edae088984432dc7d0fff816a9e016ad221a3c897a78cf79efe6c784fa9176fe.png)
